title: Principles of Microeconomics
text:
Preface
Welcome to Principles of Microeconomics: An Institutional and Social Science Perspective.
This textbook offers an analytical, empirical approach to microeconomic decision-making, price theory, market structures, and policy evaluation. It is structured around the analytical depth of Eric Chiang (Microeconomics: Principles for a Changing World, 5th ed.) and UC Berkeley Econ 1.
Use the left sidebar navigation to explore individual chapters or press s to initiate full-text keyword searches across the entire volume.

text: 1.1 Scarcity, Choice, and Opportunity Cost
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles

title: 1  Chapter 1: Foundations of Microeconomic Analysis & Core Principles
text:
Conceptual Introduction
Every day begins with a boundary you cannot escape: there are only 24 hours in a day, and your bank account holds a finite number of dollars. Yet human desires—for housing, education, travel, healthcare, clean air, and leisure—are virtually limitless. Economics exists because of this fundamental collision, known as scarcity: the condition in which limited productive resources cannot satisfy all human wants simultaneously. Because we cannot have everything, every individual, household, business, and government is forced to make choices.
Whenever you choose one option, you automatically give up the next best alternative you could have pursued with that same time or money. Economists call this sacrifice your opportunity cost. Crucially, true economic opportunity cost is wider than the cash receipt you get at a checkout counter. It combines two distinct components: explicit costs (direct out-of-pocket dollar payments) and implicit costs (the non-monetary value of foregone time, foregone wages, or alternative uses of assets you already own).
Understanding opportunity cost transforms how rational people evaluate decisions. A decision is only worthwhile if its total benefit exceeds its full economic cost—not merely its cash price. At the same time, rational decision-makers must ignore sunk costs: historical expenses that have already been paid and cannot be recovered regardless of what choice you make today. Letting unrecoverable past spending trap you into bad future choices is known as the sunk cost fallacy.






NoteClear It Up: Sunk Costs Are Not Opportunity Costs



Suppose you pay \(\$80\) for a non-refundable concert ticket, and on the night of the show a severe winter storm hits. Driving to the arena risks a car accident and three hours in freezing traffic. The \(\$80\) ticket price is a sunk cost—whether you stay home in a warm blanket or drive through the blizzard, that \(\$80\) is gone forever. Your true opportunity cost of going to the concert tonight is your safety and three hours of warm study time, not the \(\$80\) you already spent last month.




Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates scarcity and opportunity cost on a simple linear budget constraint for a college student dividing a fixed weekly budget of \(\$60\) between campus lunches (\(\$12\) each) and commuter transit day-passes (\(\$6\) each). This two-good diagram relies on three simplifying assumptions: income is fixed at \(\$60\), unit prices remain constant regardless of quantity purchased, and the student spends the entire budget.



Figure 1. Scarcity and Opportunity Cost on a Budget Line. Moving from bundle \(A(2,6)\) to bundle \(B(3,4)\) gains \(1\) additional campus lunch by sacrificing \(2\) transit day-passes, illustrating a constant opportunity cost of \(2\) passes per lunch. Point \(U(4,6)\) costs \(\$84 > \$60\) and is unaffordable.








NoteBring It Home: The True Economic Cost of a College Degree



When families evaluate the cost of attending a four-year public university, they usually focus on the bursar’s bill: tuition, campus fees, and textbooks. Yet for most full-time undergraduates, the largest single cost of higher education never appears on an invoice.

Explicit Costs: Suppose annual tuition, fees, and books total \(\$11{,}000\) per year. (Room and board are excluded here under the simplifying assumption that the student would pay similar rent and grocery bills even while working full-time.)
Implicit Costs: By attending classes full-time instead of working an entry-level full-time job paying \(\$38{,}000\) per year, the student foregoes \(\$38{,}000\) in annual wages.

Adding both components gives an illustrative annual economic opportunity cost of \(\$11{,}000 + \$38{,}000 = \mathbf{\$49{,}000}\). Assuming these amounts remain constant for four years, the total is \(\$196{,}000\). Actual costs depend on tuition, financial aid, living arrangements, work hours, and the wages a student could otherwise earn. The model predicts that lower available wages reduce the opportunity cost of full-time schooling, all else equal; it does not imply enrollment rises in every recession.




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Total Economic Cost sums explicit monetary outlays and implicit opportunity costs:
\[
\text{Total Economic Cost} = \text{Explicit Costs} + \text{Implicit Costs}
\]
Along a linear budget constraint \(P_x X + P_y Y = I\), solving for \(Y\) gives the slope-intercept form \(Y = \frac{I}{P_y} - \frac{P_x}{P_y}X\). The vertical intercept \(\frac{I}{P_y}\) is the maximum affordable quantity of \(Y\), and the magnitude of the slope is the constant opportunity cost of one unit of Good \(X\):
\[
\text{Opportunity Cost of } 1 \text{ unit of } X = \left|\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}\right| = \frac{P_x}{P_y}
\]
In Figure 1, \(12X + 6Y = 60\) rearranges to \(Y = 10 - 2X\), so each additional lunch costs \(\frac{\$12}{\$6} = 2\) transit day-passes.






NoteWork It Out: Calculating Economic vs. Accounting Cost



Problem: Maya currently works as a graphic designer earning \(\$65{,}000\) per year. She is considering quitting her job to launch her own independent design studio. In her first year, she expects to pay \(\$18{,}000\) for studio rent, \(\$7{,}000\) for software and equipment leases, and \(\$15{,}000\) for marketing and supplies. Additionally, she must move \(\$20{,}000\) out of a personal savings account that was earning \(5\%\) annual interest to hold as refundable studio deposits and working capital (recovered if she closes the business). Calculate Maya’s explicit costs, implicit costs, and total economic cost for Year 1.
Step-by-Step Solution:

Sum All Explicit Out-of-Pocket Costs: Add the direct monetary payments required to run the studio:

\[
\text{Explicit Costs} = \$18{,}000 + \$7{,}000 + \$15{,}000 = \mathbf{\$40{,}000}
\]

Calculate Implicit Foregone Interest: Because the \(\$20{,}000\) deposit/working-capital principal is recoverable, only the foregone interest is an annual economic cost:

\[
\text{Foregone Interest} = \$20{,}000 \times 0.05 = \$1{,}000
\]

Sum All Implicit Opportunity Costs: Combine Maya’s foregone salary with her foregone savings interest:

\[
\text{Implicit Costs} = \$65{,}000 + \$1{,}000 = \mathbf{\$66{,}000}
\]

Compute Total Economic Cost:

\[
\text{Total Economic Cost} = \$40{,}000 + \$66{,}000 = \mathbf{\$106{,}000}
\]
Conclusion: Even if Maya’s studio brings in \(\$80{,}000\) in client revenue—giving her an accounting profit of \(\$80{,}000 - \$40{,}000 = \$40{,}000\)—she would suffer an economic loss of \(\$80{,}000 - \$106{,}000 = -\$26{,}000\) compared to keeping her salaried job.








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus of Opportunity Cost and Slopes



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: For any smooth trade-off frontier \(Y = f(X)\), the instantaneous (marginal) opportunity cost of Good \(X\) in terms of Good \(Y\) is the absolute value of the first derivative, \(\left|\frac{dY}{dX}\right|\). For the linear budget constraint \(P_x X + P_y Y = I\) with fixed prices and income, differentiating implicitly yields:
\[
P_x\,dX + P_y\,dY = 0 \implies \frac{dY}{dX} = -\frac{P_x}{P_y}
\]
Because \(\frac{d^2 Y}{dX^2} = 0\), the opportunity cost \(\frac{P_x}{P_y}\) is constant at every bundle along the line. By contrast, when resources are specialized (as on a bowed-out Production Possibilities Frontier in Chapter 2), \(\frac{dY}{dX} < 0\) and \(\frac{d^2 Y}{dX^2} < 0\), so marginal opportunity cost \(\left|\frac{dY}{dX}\right|\) rises as \(X\) expands.

section: 1.2 Marginal Decision-Making and Incentives
text:
1.2 Marginal Decision-Making and Incentives

Conceptual Introduction
Most real-world economic decisions are not ``all-or-nothing’’ ultimatums. A student rarely chooses between studying zero hours or 24 hours straight; they decide whether to study one more hour tonight. A coffee shop does not decide between brewing zero cups or one million cups; it decides whether to stay open one extra hour in the evening. Economists analyze these incremental adjustments through marginal analysis, comparing the marginal benefit (\(MB\)) of one additional unit of an activity against its marginal cost (\(MC\)).
The basic rule is straightforward: as long as the extra benefit of one more unit exceeds its extra cost (\(MB > MC\)), expanding the activity increases net benefit. If the extra cost is greater (\(MC > MB\)), scale back. For a smooth, interior choice, net benefit is maximized where \(MB=MC\); with indivisible choices, compare successive units and stop before the next unit whose marginal cost exceeds its marginal benefit.
Because rational agents weigh marginal benefits against marginal costs, changing either side of that ledger predictably alters human behavior. Economists call any reward or penalty that shifts \(MB\) or \(MC\) an incentive. When policymakers introduce taxes, subsidies, fines, or regulations, people respond to the new incentives—sometimes in clever, unintended ways that backfire against the policy’s original goal.






NoteClear It Up: Marginal Cost Is Not Average Cost



Students frequently confuse average cost (total cost divided by total units produced) with marginal cost (the extra cost of adding one more unit). Average cost spreads already-committed fixed expenses across all units, whereas marginal cost isolates only the new resources required for the next unit. When deciding whether to expand an activity by one unit, compare marginal benefit to marginal cost—not average cost.




Visual Representation
Figure 2 illustrates marginal optimization using hypothetical linear schedules measured in dollar-equivalent value per hour ($/hr), holding exam difficulty and prior preparation constant (ceteris paribus). Assuming study time \(H\) is continuously divisible, the downward-sloping Marginal Benefit curve intersects the upward-sloping Marginal Cost curve at \(H^* = 4\) study hours.



Figure 2. Marginal Optimization Rule. Under the illustrative linear schedules, marginal benefit (\(MB = 20 - 3H\)) and marginal cost (\(MC = 2H\)) intersect at \(H^* = 4\) hours, where both equal \(\$8/\text{hr}\). At \(H = 2\), \(MB (\$14) > MC (\$4)\); beyond \(H^* = 4\), \(MC > MB\).








NoteBring It Home: Seatbelt Laws and the Peltzman Effect



Beginning January 1, 1968, federal safety standards required new U.S. passenger cars to have seat belts. The goal was to improve safety. Economist Sam Peltzman (1975) argued that drivers might respond to some safety improvements by taking greater risks:

By making car crashes far more survivable for the driver, safety equipment lowered the marginal cost to a driver of speeding or braking late.
If drivers perceive lower personal risk, some may drive faster or more aggressively, offsetting part of the safety benefit and shifting risk toward people outside the vehicle.

This proposed behavioral response is often called the Peltzman effect. It is a hypothesis about incentives, not a claim that seat belts generally increase fatalities; the size and distribution of any response depend on evidence and context.




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Marginal Benefit and Marginal Cost measure the change in total benefit (\(TB\)) and total cost (\(TC\)) from a one-unit increase in quantity (\(\Delta Q = 1\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
MB &= \frac{\Delta TB}{\Delta Q}, \\
MC &= \frac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q}, \\
\text{Interior optimum: } & MB = MC
\end{aligned}
\]
Applying this rule to Figure 2, setting \(MB = MC\) gives \(20 - 3H = 2H \implies 5H = 20 \implies H^* = 4\) hours, with \(MB = MC = 2(4) = \$8/\text{hr}\).






NoteWork It Out: Pricing a Last-Minute Standby Airline Seat



Problem: A regional airline operates a 150-seat flight from San Francisco to Seattle. Total fixed and fuel costs for the flight equal \(\$15{,}000\), which works out to an average cost of \(\$15{,}000 / 150 = \$100\) per seat. Ten minutes before boarding closes, 12 seats remain empty. Adding one standby passenger requires only \(\$15\) in extra jet fuel, cabin snacks, and baggage handling. A standby passenger offers to pay \(\$65\) for a ticket. Assuming selling this standby ticket does not displace or cannibalize any full-fare passengers, should the airline sell the seat?
Step-by-Step Solution:

Identify Sunk Costs vs. Marginal Cost (\(MC\)): The \(\$15{,}000\) cost to fly the plane is already committed regardless of whether the empty seat is filled. The incremental cost of boarding one additional passenger is:

\[
MC = \mathbf{\$15}
\]

Identify Marginal Benefit (\(MB\)): The additional revenue collected from selling the standby ticket is:

\[
MB = \mathbf{\$65}
\]

Apply the Marginal Decision Rule (\(MB\) vs. \(MC\)): Compare marginal benefit to marginal cost (ignoring the irrelevant \(\$100\) average cost):

\[
MB\ (\$65) > MC\ (\$15) \implies \text{Net Operating Gain} = \$65 - \$15 = \mathbf{+\$50}
\]
Conclusion: Yes—the airline should sell the seat. Although the \(\$65\) fare is below the \(\$100\) average cost per seat, it exceeds the \(\$15\) incremental cost and adds \(\$50\) to profit.








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus of Net Benefit Maximization



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Let Total Benefit be \(TB(Q)\) and Total Cost be \(TC(Q)\). Net Benefit is \(NB(Q) = TB(Q) - TC(Q)\). Maximizing \(NB(Q)\) requires setting the first derivative with respect to \(Q\) equal to zero:
\[
\frac{d(NB)}{dQ} = \frac{d(TB)}{dQ} - \frac{d(TC)}{dQ} = 0 \implies MB(Q^*) = MC(Q^*)
\]
The second-order sufficient condition for a maximum requires \(\frac{d^2(NB)}{dQ^2} = \frac{d(MB)}{dQ} - \frac{d(MC)}{dQ} < 0\), which holds whenever \(MC\) crosses \(MB\) from below (such as downward-sloping \(MB\) and upward-sloping \(MC\)). In Figure 2, integrating \(MB = 20 - 3H\) and \(MC = 2H\) from zero gives \(TB(H) = 20H - 1.5H^2\) and \(TC(H) = H^2\), so \(NB(H) = 20H - 2.5H^2\). Setting \(\frac{d(NB)}{dH} = 20 - 5H = 0\) confirms \(H^* = 4\), \(\frac{d^2(NB)}{dH^2} = -5 < 0\), and maximum net benefit \(NB(4) = 20(4) - 2.5(16) = \$40\) (equal to the triangle area \(\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times \$20 = \$40\)).

section: 1.3 Economic Models, Ceteris Paribus, and Methodology
text:
1.3 Economic Models, Ceteris Paribus, and Methodology

Conceptual Introduction
The real economy involves millions of consumers, firms, prices, weather events, and policy changes interacting simultaneously. To make sense of this complexity without getting lost in irrelevant detail, economists build simplified analytical maps called economic models. Just as a subway map omits every tree and storefront so you can clearly trace train routes, an economic model strips away secondary noise to isolate how one specific variable affects another.
To test a single cause-and-effect link cleanly, economists rely on the foundational assumption of ceteris paribus—a Latin phrase meaning ``all other things held constant.’’ When an economist states that a lower price increases the quantity of coffee demanded ceteris paribus, they mean quantity rises assuming consumer income, weather, competitor prices, and tastes remain frozen. Without ceteris paribus, it is impossible to tell whether coffee sales rose because of a price discount or because a winter cold snap hit the city.
Finally, rigorous economic analysis separates two distinct types of statements:

Positive Economics: Testable statements about what is or what may happen if a policy changes (e.g., ``A minimum-wage increase may affect teen restaurant employment’’). The direction and size of any effect are empirical questions.
Normative Economics: Value judgments and opinions about what ought to be (e.g., ``The government should raise the minimum wage to reduce poverty’’). Normative claims depend on ethical priorities and cannot be settled by data alone.







NoteClear It Up: Positive Does Not Mean ``True,’’ and Correlation Is Not Causation



Two methodological traps trip up introductory students. First, a positive statement does not have to be factually correct—claiming Raising tuition always increases college enrollment''* is a positive statement because it can be tested and refuted with data, whereas *Tuition should be free’’ is normative. Second, observing two variables move together (correlation) does not prove one causes the other: if ice cream sales and swimming accidents rise together in July, warm summer weather—an omitted third variable—drives both.




Visual Representation
Figure 3 maps the economy’s core interactions using a simplified two-sector Circular Flow Diagram. To isolate the fundamental exchange between households and firms, this baseline model intentionally abstracts away from government taxation and spending, financial intermediaries, and international trade.



Figure 3. The Circular Flow Model. Solid outer arrows trace dollar flows (consumer spending becoming firm revenue, and factor payments becoming household income), while dashed inner arrows trace physical goods and productive inputs.








NoteBring It Home: Separating Micro from Macro in Housing Policy



Economics divides into two complementary lenses:

Microeconomics examines individual markets, households, and firms—such as how a city’s zoning law affects apartment rents in San Francisco or how rideshare drivers respond to surge pricing.
Macroeconomics examines the economy as a whole—such as national GDP growth, Federal Reserve interest-rate policy, and U.S. unemployment rates.

For example, a macroeconomic study of higher mortgage rates might ask how home construction changes nationally, while a microeconomic study of a local housing market might ask how individual buyers adjust between owning and renting. These are questions a model can organize; establishing causation requires empirical evidence beyond the model itself.




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
A linear model isolates a dependent variable \(Y\) as a function of an explanatory variable \(X\), holding all other determinants fixed inside the intercept \(a\):
\[
Y = a + bX \qquad (\text{holding all non-}X\text{ factors constant})
\]






NoteWork It Out: Applying Ceteris Paribus to Public Transit Ridership



Problem: Suppose a city’s monthly transit ridership \(R\) (in thousands of rides) depends linearly on the subway fare \(F\) (in dollars) and average local gasoline prices \(G\) (in dollars per gallon) according to the illustrative model:
\[
R = 120 - 15F + 10G
\]
Using ceteris paribus, calculate monthly ridership when the fare is \(F = \$2.00\) and gas is \(G = \$4.00\), and find the pure effect of raising the fare to \(F = \$3.00\) while holding gas prices constant.
Step-by-Step Solution:

Freeze the Non-Fare Variable (\(G = \$4.00\)): Holding \(G = 4.00\) constant collapses the model into the single-variable linear form \(R = a + bF\):

\[
R = 120 + 10(4.00) - 15F = 160 - 15F
\]

Compute Baseline Ridership (\(F = \$2.00\), \(G = \$4.00\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
R_1 &= 120 - 15(2.00) + 10(4.00) \\
&= 120 - 30 + 40 \\
&= \mathbf{130\text{ thousand rides}}
\end{aligned}
\]

Apply Ceteris Paribus (\(F = \$3.00\), holding \(G = \$4.00\) fixed):

\[
\begin{aligned}
R_2 &= 120 - 15(3.00) + 10(4.00) \\
&= 120 - 45 + 40 \\
&= \mathbf{115\text{ thousand rides}}
\end{aligned}
\]

Isolate the Ceteris Paribus Effect of the Fare Hike:

\[
\Delta R = R_2 - R_1 = 115 - 130 = \mathbf{-15\text{ thousand rides}}
\]
Conclusion: Holding gasoline prices constant within this model, each \(\$1.00\) increase in subway fare reduces monthly transit ridership by \(15{,}000\) rides.








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Partial Derivatives as Formal Ceteris Paribus



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: In multivariable calculus, the ceteris paribus assumption is formalized by the partial derivative, which differentiates a function with respect to one explanatory variable while treating all other variables as constants. For the transit ridership model \(R(F, G) = 120 - 15F + 10G\):
\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial F} = -15 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{\partial R}{\partial G} = +10
\]
When both fare and gas price change simultaneously, the total differential separates their individual contributions:
\[
dR = \frac{\partial R}{\partial F}\,dF + \frac{\partial R}{\partial G}\,dG = -15\,dF + 10\,dG
\]




Selected References

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. ``Seat Belts in New Passenger Cars’’ (interpretation 11695JEG; requirement effective January 1, 1968). https://www.nhtsa.gov/interpretations/11695jeg
Peltzman, Sam. 1975. ``The Effects of Automobile Safety Regulation.’’ Journal of Political Economy 83(4): 677–725. https://doi.org/10.1086/260352

text:
Learning Outcomes and Key Terms
Upon completing this chapter, students should be able to:
Key Terms: Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF), productive efficiency, allocative efficiency, Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost, Marginal Rate of Transformation (\(MRT\)), economic growth, absolute advantage, comparative advantage, specialization, Terms of Trade (\(TOT\)), Consumption Possibilities Frontier (\(CPF\)), autarky.

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
text:
Conceptual Introduction
No economy—not even the wealthiest nation on earth—has enough workers, factories, farmland, and energy to produce unlimited quantities of every good simultaneously. To visualize this society-wide scarcity constraint, economists construct the Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF), a curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce when all available resources and technology are fully and efficiently employed.
Every point on or near the PPF reveals a critical truth about how an economy is performing:

Productive Efficiency (Points on the Frontier): The economy is squeezing the maximum possible output from its existing workers and machines. Along the frontier, producing more of Good \(X\) is impossible without giving up some of Good \(Y\).
Inefficiency (Points Inside the Frontier): The economy is producing below its potential due to unemployed workers, idle factories, or misallocated resources. Moving from an interior point to the frontier allows society to gain more of both goods without any sacrifice.
Unattainable Output (Points Outside the Frontier): Combinations beyond the boundary cannot be achieved today given current labor, capital, and technology.

Because societies must choose which point along the frontier best matches citizen preferences, economists also distinguish productive efficiency (producing at lowest possible cost on the curve) from allocative efficiency (choosing the specific point on the curve where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, \(MB = MC\)).
Real-World Connection. During the 2020 recession, the U.S. unemployment rate reached \(14.7\%\) in April, its highest seasonally adjusted level in the BLS series dating to 1948, as reported in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ The Employment Situation—April 2020 (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/empsit_05082020.htm). In a PPF model, unused workers and capacity are represented by a point inside the frontier; the diagram is conceptual rather than a measured location. Wartime conversion of civilian production to military production is another illustration: at full use of resources, shifting output toward one good requires sacrificing some of another.


Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates a bowed-out Production Possibilities Frontier comparing clean-energy wind turbines (\(X\)) against commercial cargo ships (\(Y\)), marking efficient, inefficient, and unattainable allocations.






NoteClear It Up: Productive Efficiency vs. Allocative Efficiency



Every single point on the PPF is productively efficient because no resources are wasted. However, only one specific point on the PPF is allocatively efficient—the mix of goods society actually wants most (\(MB = MC\)). Producing \(100\%\) left-handed baseball gloves and zero right-handed gloves is productively efficient if no leather is wasted, yet completely allocatively inefficient!





Figure 1. The Production Possibilities Frontier. Points \(B\) and \(C\) lie on the frontier and represent full employment and productive efficiency. Point \(U\) lies inside the frontier (idle resources), while point \(N\) is currently unattainable.




Mathematical Foundation
Along a linear PPF connecting vertical intercept \(Y_{\max}\) and horizontal intercept \(X_{\max}\), the Marginal Rate of Transformation (\(MRT\))—the opportunity cost of producing one additional unit of \(X\)—is the absolute slope of the line:
\[
MRT = \left|\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}\right| = \frac{Y_{\max}}{X_{\max}}
\]
Worked Problem: A small island nation can produce a maximum of \(200\) tons of mangoes per month if it devotes all labor to farming, or \(50\) fishing boats per month if it devotes all labor to boatbuilding. Assuming a linear PPF with constant opportunity cost:

Write the equation of the island’s PPF with mangoes (\(M\)) on the vertical axis and boats (\(B\)) on the horizontal axis.
Calculate the opportunity cost of building \(1\) fishing boat and the opportunity cost of harvesting \(1\) ton of mangoes.
Determine whether the bundle \((B = 30, M = 90)\) is efficient, inefficient, or unattainable.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Write the Linear PPF Equation: The vertical intercept is \(M_{\max} = 200\) and the horizontal intercept is \(B_{\max} = 50\). The slope is \(-\frac{200}{50} = -4\):

\[
M = 200 - 4B
\]

Compute Opportunity Costs:

\[
\text{Opportunity Cost of } 1 \text{ Boat} = \frac{200\text{ mangoes}}{50\text{ boats}} = \mathbf{4\text{ tons of mangoes}}
\]
\[
\text{Opportunity Cost of } 1 \text{ Ton of Mangoes} = \frac{50\text{ boats}}{200\text{ mangoes}} = \mathbf{0.25\text{ fishing boats}}
\]

Evaluate Bundle \((B = 30, M = 90)\): Plug \(B = 30\) into the PPF equation to find the maximum possible mango output:

\[
M_{\text{frontier}} = 200 - 4(30) = 200 - 120 = 80\text{ tons of mangoes}
\]
Because \(90 > 80\), the bundle \((30, 90)\) lies outside the frontier and is unattainable.
Conclusion: Building \(30\) boats leaves only enough resources to harvest \(80\) tons of mangoes, so producing \(90\) tons is impossible without new technology or more workers.

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: 2.2 Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost and Economic Growth
text:
2.2 Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost and Economic Growth

Conceptual Introduction
Why is the PPF in Figure 1 bowed outward (concave to the origin) rather than drawn as a straight line? Because economic resources are not equally suited to producing every good. Farmland in California’s Central Valley is extraordinarily productive for growing almonds and tomatoes, whereas software engineers in Silicon Valley are specialized in writing code.
When an economy first begins shifting resources out of agriculture and into software, it transfers the least fertile farmland and the most tech-savvy workers first—giving up very few crops for a huge gain in software. However, as society pushes further toward producing almost exclusively software, it must eventually pull prime agricultural land and veteran farmers out of farming, causing crop output to plummet for only a tiny gain in code. This universal pattern is the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost: as production of one good expands, the opportunity cost of producing each additional unit rises.
Over time, an economy can break through its existing frontier via economic growth—an outward shift of the entire PPF. Economic growth is driven by three engines: (1) expanding the capital stock through investment in machines and infrastructure (capital deepening), (2) growing the labor force or improving worker skills (human capital), and (3) advancing technology.
Real-World Connection. A semiconductor fabrication plant requires land, skilled labor, equipment, and electricity that could have been used elsewhere while the plant is built. If the completed facility adds productive capacity, this investment can expand future production possibilities; the scale of that effect depends on the resources invested and the facility’s productivity.


Visual Representation
Figure 2 illustrates how prioritizing capital goods investment today shifts the entire PPF outward tomorrow, expanding future production possibilities.



Figure 2. Economic Growth Shifts the PPF Outward. Investing in physical capital, human capital, and technological innovation expands an economy’s productive capacity from the 2026 frontier to the 2036 frontier.




Mathematical Foundation
Along a curved PPF, the opportunity cost between two discrete points \((X_1, Y_1)\) and \((X_2, Y_2)\) is computed by dividing the vertical drop in \(Y\) by the horizontal gain in \(X\):
\[
\text{Opportunity Cost of } X \text{ over interval} = \left|\frac{Y_2 - Y_1}{X_2 - X_1}\right|
\]
Worked Problem: An economy produces solar panels (\(X\)) and electric buses (\(Y\)) along a bowed-out PPF with the following efficient production combinations:

Point A: \(0\) solar panels, \(100\) electric buses
Point B: \(20\) solar panels, \(90\) electric buses
Point C: \(40\) solar panels, \(65\) electric buses
Point D: \(60\) solar panels, \(0\) electric buses

Calculate the per-unit opportunity cost of producing solar panels as the economy moves from \(A \to B\), from \(B \to C\), and from \(C \to D\).
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Interval \(A \to B\):

\[
\text{Opportunity Cost} = \left|\frac{90 - 100}{20 - 0}\right| = \frac{10}{20} = \mathbf{0.50\text{ buses per solar panel}}
\]

Interval \(B \to C\):

\[
\text{Opportunity Cost} = \left|\frac{65 - 90}{40 - 20}\right| = \frac{25}{20} = \mathbf{1.25\text{ buses per solar panel}}
\]

Interval \(C \to D\):

\[
\text{Opportunity Cost} = \left|\frac{0 - 65}{60 - 40}\right| = \frac{65}{20} = \mathbf{3.25\text{ buses per solar panel}}
\]
Conclusion: Per-unit opportunity cost rises from \(0.50 \to 1.25 \to 3.25\) buses per panel, confirming the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus of Concave PPFs



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Suppose a bowed-out PPF is described by the quadratic equation \(Y = 100 - \frac{1}{4}X^2\) for \(X \in [0, 20]\). The instantaneous Marginal Rate of Transformation (\(MRT\)) is the absolute value of the first derivative:
\[
MRT(X) = \left|\frac{dY}{dX}\right| = \frac{1}{2}X
\]
Because the second derivative of \(MRT(X)\) with respect to \(X\) is \(\frac{d(MRT)}{dX} = \frac{1}{2} > 0\), opportunity cost strictly increases with \(X\) at every point along the frontier.

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: 2.3 Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
text:
2.3 Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

Conceptual Introduction
Why do individuals, cities, and nations specialize in specific careers or industries and trade with one another instead of producing everything themselves? In 1817, economist David Ricardo proved that mutually beneficial trade does not require being the most productive producer in the world. Instead, trade is governed by comparative advantage.
To see why, keep two concepts strictly separate:

Absolute Advantage: The ability to produce a larger quantity of a good using the same amount of inputs (or the same output using fewer labor hours).
Comparative Advantage: The ability to produce a good at a lower domestic opportunity cost than a trading partner.

Even if one person or country holds an absolute advantage in every activity, it is mathematically impossible for one party to have a comparative advantage in both goods (unless their opportunity costs are identical). When each party specializes in the good where its opportunity cost is lower and trades at a mutually agreeable Terms of Trade (\(TOT\)), each gains access to consumption bundles beyond its domestic PPF. The expanded choice set allows each party to choose a bundle it prefers to its autarky bundle.
Real-World Connection. The contrast between technology firms in Silicon Valley and agricultural production in the Central Valley offers a local illustration of specialization. Whether either region has a comparative advantage in a particular good depends on its opportunity cost, not simply on its reputation or absolute output.


Visual Representation
Figure 3 shows Region A’s domestic PPF and its consumption possibilities frontier when it can trade at 2 tons of wheat per semiconductor.



Figure 3. Trade expands Region A’s feasible consumption set. After specializing in semiconductors, Region A exports 10 units for 20 tons of wheat at a terms of trade of 2 tons per semiconductor; the resulting bundle lies outside its domestic PPF.




Mathematical Foundation
For trade between Region A and Region B to benefit both sides, the Terms of Trade (\(TOT\)) for \(1\) unit of Good \(X\) must settle strictly between their two domestic opportunity costs:
\[
\text{Opportunity Cost of } X \text{ in Region A} < TOT < \text{Opportunity Cost of } X \text{ in Region B}
\]
Worked Problem: In a single workday, Region A can produce either \(40\) units of semiconductors (\(X\)) or \(40\) tons of wheat (\(Y\)). Region B can produce either \(10\) units of semiconductors (\(X\)) or \(30\) tons of wheat (\(Y\)).

Identify which region holds the absolute advantage in each good.
Calculate domestic opportunity costs and identify comparative advantage.
Verify that a Terms of Trade of \(1\text{ semiconductor} = 2\text{ tons of wheat}\) benefits both regions if Region A trades \(10\) semiconductors to Region B.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Determine Absolute Advantage: Region A produces more semiconductors (\(40 > 10\)) and more wheat (\(40 > 30\)), so Region A holds the absolute advantage in both goods.
Calculate Domestic Opportunity Costs:
Region A: One semiconductor costs \(\frac{40}{40}=1\) ton of wheat; one ton of wheat costs \(\frac{40}{40}=1\) semiconductor.
Region B: One semiconductor costs \(\frac{30}{10}=3\) tons of wheat; one ton of wheat costs \(\frac{10}{30}=\frac{1}{3}\) semiconductor.

Comparing opportunity costs:

Region A has comparative advantage in semiconductors because \(1 < 3\) tons of wheat per semiconductor.
Region B has comparative advantage in wheat because \(\frac{1}{3} < 1\) semiconductor per ton of wheat.
Verify Gains at \(TOT = 2\text{ tons of wheat per semiconductor}\):
Region A specializes in semiconductors and produces \((40\ X,0\ Y)\). It exports \(10\ X\) and imports \(10 \times 2=20\ Y\), consuming \((30\ X,20\ Y)\). Its comparison bundle \((30\ X,10\ Y)\) is feasible on its domestic PPF, so trade makes 10 more tons of wheat available at the same semiconductor consumption.
Region B specializes in wheat and produces \((0\ X,30\ Y)\). It imports \(10\ X\) and exports \(10 \times 2=20\ Y\), consuming \((10\ X,10\ Y)\). Its comparison bundle \((10\ X,0\ Y)\) is feasible on its domestic PPF, so trade makes 10 more tons of wheat available at the same semiconductor consumption.

Conclusion: The terms of trade (\(2\) tons of wheat per semiconductor) lie between Region A’s opportunity cost (\(1\) ton) and Region B’s (\(3\) tons). Given the stated comparison bundles and the assumption that more of a good is preferred to less, each region can gain 10 tons of wheat at the same semiconductor consumption. The trade bundles lie beyond each region’s domestic PPF.

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
text: 3.1 Demand: Consumer Valuation and Curve Shifts
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
text:
Conceptual Introduction
Every time you decide whether to buy a \(\$5\) campus iced coffee, stream a movie, or wait for a textbook sale, you participate in a market where a single-product price guides everyday choices. Throughout this chapter, \(P\) denotes the market price of one specific product (measured in dollars per unit), which is strictly distinct from economy-wide aggregate price indexes (such as the Consumer Price Index or GDP Deflator) studied in Macroeconomics. On the buyer’s side, the Law of Demand states that, ceteris paribus (holding all other factors constant), when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. Two microeconomic forces drive this inverse relationship: the substitution effect (a higher price makes alternative products relatively cheaper, prompting consumers to switch) and the income effect (a higher price reduces the real purchasing power of a household’s fixed paycheck).
Keeping a change in quantity demanded strictly separate from a change in demand is one of the most important analytical habits in economics. A change in the product’s own price moves consumers up or down along a fixed demand curve. By contrast, a change in any non-price determinant shifts the entire demand curve to the right (an increase in demand at every price) or to the left (a decrease in demand at every price).
Five major non-price shifters move the entire demand curve:

Consumer Income: Higher income shifts demand rightward for normal goods (such as fresh produce or airline travel) and leftward for inferior goods (such as instant ramen or intercity bus tickets).
Prices of Related Goods: A price hike for a substitute (e.g., Pepsi) shifts demand rightward for the rival good (Coca-Cola); a price hike for a complement (e.g., smartphone data plans) shifts demand leftward for smartphones.
Tastes and Preferences: Health studies, cultural trends, and advertising.
Buyer Expectations: Anticipating higher future prices or future raises boosts current demand today.
Number of Buyers: Population growth or demographic expansion shifts market demand outward.



Visual Representation
Figure 1 contrasts a movement along a stationary demand curve (\(A \to B\), caused by a drop in own price) against a rightward shift of the entire demand curve (\(D_1 \to D_2\), caused by a non-price determinant such as higher income).






NoteClear It Up: Never Say ``Price Rose, So Demand Fell’’



When the price of concert tickets jumps from \(\$60\) to \(\$90\), the demand curve does not shift! Buyers simply move upward along the existing demand curve to a smaller quantity demanded. Only non-price factors (income, substitutes, complements, tastes, expectations, or buyer count) shift the demand curve itself.





Figure 1. Movement Along Demand vs. Shift of Demand. A price drop from \(\$80\) to \(\$60\) moves buyers along \(D_1\) from \(A\) to \(B\) (a change in quantity demanded). Higher consumer income shifts the entire curve from \(D_1\) to \(D_2\), raising quantity demanded at \(\$60\) from \(20\) to \(30\) (point \(C\)).




Real-World Application: Electric Vehicle Demand and Charging Networks
As a hypothetical example, an EV sticker-price reduction moves buyers along the demand curve when the price shown on the vertical axis is the price they pay. More fast-charging access can raise the value of owning an EV, while a buyer tax credit lowers the buyer’s effective price relative to the sticker price. When a graph uses the sticker price, these non-sticker-price changes can be represented as a demand shift; the tax credit is not itself a change in the posted sticker price.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Assuming linear demand and ceteris paribus (all non-price determinants held fixed), a direct demand function is written as \(Q_d = a - bP\) and inverted for graphing as:
\[
P = \frac{a}{b} - \frac{1}{b}Q_d \qquad (a > 0, \; b > 0)
\]
Work It Out: Linear Demand, Choke Price, and Demand Shifts
Monthly demand for campus cold-brew subscriptions is given by \(Q_d = 400 - 10P\), where \(P\) is the monthly price in dollars.

Rewrite the demand equation in inverse form (\(P\) as a function of \(Q_d\)) and find the choke price.
Compute quantity demanded at \(P_1 = \$25\) and \(P_2 = \$15\).
Suppose midterms begin and student demand increases by \(80\) subscriptions at every price level. Write the new direct demand equation.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Invert the Demand Equation: Solve \(Q_d = 400 - 10P\) for \(P\):

\[
10P = 400 - Q_d \implies P = \mathbf{40 - 0.1Q_d}
\]
Setting \(Q_d = 0\) gives the choke price \(P_{\text{choke}} = \mathbf{\$40}\).

Calculate Quantities Along the Original Demand Curve:

\[
Q_d(25) = 400 - 10(25) = \mathbf{150\text{ subscriptions}}, \qquad Q_d(15) = 400 - 10(15) = \mathbf{250\text{ subscriptions}}
\]

Shift the Demand Equation Rightward by \(+80\) Units: Add \(80\) to the horizontal intercept \(a\):

\[
Q_d^{\text{new}} = (400 + 80) - 10P = \mathbf{480 - 10P}
\]
Conclusion: Lowering price from \(\$25\) to \(\$15\) increases quantity demanded by \(100\) units along the curve, whereas midterm fatigue shifts the entire demand curve rightward by \(80\) units at every price.

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
section: 3.2 Supply: Production Costs and Curve Shifts
text:
3.2 Supply: Production Costs and Curve Shifts

Conceptual Introduction
Imagine a neighborhood bakery deciding whether to run its ovens for an extra late-afternoon batch of sourdough loaves: baking more requires overtime wages and extra energy, so the owner will expand output only if the market price per loaf is high enough to cover those added costs. On the seller’s side of the market, the Law of Supply states that, ceteris paribus, higher market prices induce firms to offer a larger quantity for sale, while lower prices reduce quantity supplied. In many short-run settings, some inputs are fixed; diminishing marginal productivity can then raise the marginal cost (\(MC\)) of additional units. Firms are willing to supply those units when the market price covers their marginal cost. This is one common reason for an upward-sloping supply curve, not a universal technological law.
Just as with demand, a change in the product’s own price causes a movement along a stationary supply curve, whereas a change in underlying production conditions shifts the entire supply curve:

Input Prices: Higher wages, raw material costs, or energy prices raise marginal cost and shift supply leftward (upward).
Technology: Automation and process innovations lower production costs and shift supply rightward.
Taxes and Subsidies: A per-unit business tax raises marginal cost (shifting supply leftward), while a production subsidy lowers marginal cost (shifting supply rightward).
Seller Expectations and Number of Sellers: New firms entering an industry shift market supply rightward.







NoteClear It Up: Why an ``Upward’’ Supply Shift Means Less Supply



Always describe curve shifts as rightward (increase) or leftward (decrease) rather than up'' ordown.’’ When input costs rise, sellers require a higher minimum price for every unit—moving the supply curve vertically upward, which is a leftward shift showing smaller quantity supplied at every given price.




Visual Representation
Figure 2 shows how a technological breakthrough lowers marginal production cost at every output level, shifting the supply curve rightward from \(S_1\) to \(S_2\).



Figure 2. Rightward Shift of Supply. Cost-reducing technology shifts supply from \(S_1\) to \(S_2\), expanding the quantity sellers are willing to supply at \(\$60\) from \(20\) units to \(25\) units.




Real-World Application: Lithium Batteries and Coffee Harvests
The U.S. Department of Energy estimates that light-duty electric-vehicle lithium-ion battery-pack costs fell 90% from 2008 to 2023 in 2023 dollars, from \(\$1{,}415\) to \(\$139\) per usable kilowatt-hour for production at a scale of at least 100{,}000 units per year. The estimate attributes the decline to improvements in technology and chemistry and to increased production volume. Lower unit costs can shift EV battery-pack supply right, all else equal; this estimate is for vehicle packs, not grid-scale storage.
Weather can affect agricultural supply, but the net outcome should not be assumed. The USDA reported severe drought and fires in Brazil from July to September 2024 and expected effects on the 2024/25 coffee harvest. Its forecast nevertheless put total Brazilian coffee production 0.2% above the previous season. This case illustrates why a supply explanation must account for the overall harvest, not just one adverse input condition.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
A linear supply function with a nonnegative minimum supply price is:
\[
Q_s = d(P-P_{\min}) \quad \text{for } P \ge P_{\min}, \qquad
P = P_{\min} + \frac{1}{d}Q_s \quad (d>0).
\]
For prices below \(P_{\min}\), this simple model sets quantity supplied to zero. This avoids interpreting a negative algebraic quantity as actual market supply.
Work It Out: Linear Supply and Input-Cost Shifts
Local bakeries supply artisan loaves according to \(Q_s = -40 + 8P\) for \(P \ge \$5\).

Find the inverse supply equation and minimum supply price \(P_{\min}\).
Suppose flour and electricity prices rise, increasing sellers’ minimum acceptable price by \(\$3\) per loaf at every quantity. Write the new inverse and direct supply equations.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Invert the Supply Equation:

\[
8P = 40 + Q_s \implies P = \mathbf{5 + 0.125Q_s}
\]
At \(Q_s = 0\), the minimum supply price is \(P_{\min} = \mathbf{\$5\text{ per loaf}}\).

Shift Supply Upward (Leftward) by \(+\$3\) per Loaf: Add \(\$3\) to the inverse supply intercept:

\[
P^{\text{new}} = (5 + 3) + 0.125Q_s = \mathbf{8 + 0.125Q_s}
\]
Solve for the new quantity schedule:
\[
P-8=0.125Q_s^{\text{new}}
\implies Q_s^{\text{new}}=8(P-8)=-64+8P.
\]
Restricting quantity supplied to nonnegative values gives:
\[
Q_s^{\text{new}} =
\begin{cases}
0, & P < \$8,\\
-64 + 8P, & P \ge \$8.
\end{cases}
\]
Conclusion: Higher input prices raise the minimum supply price to \(\$8\) per loaf. At prices of \(\$8\) or more, the new linear schedule supplies 24 fewer loaves than the old schedule; below \(\$8\), the new schedule supplies zero.

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
section: 3.3 Market Equilibrium and Comparative Statics
text:
3.3 Market Equilibrium and Comparative Statics

Conceptual Introduction
When buyers and sellers interact freely, the market converges toward market equilibrium—the unique price \(P^*\) where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied (\(Q_d = Q_s\)). At any price above \(P^*\), sellers produce more than buyers want to purchase, creating a surplus (excess supply) that pressures sellers to cut prices. At any price below \(P^*\), buyers want more units than sellers offer, creating a shortage (excess demand) that bids prices upward. Only at \((Q^*, P^*)\) does the market clear with zero upward or downward pressure on price.
To predict how equilibrium responds when real-world events disturb the market—an exercise called comparative statics—follow a strict three-step protocol: (1) identify whether the event shifts Demand, Supply, or both; (2) determine the direction of the shift (rightward or leftward); and (3) compare the new intersection \((Q_2^*, P_2^*)\) against the original equilibrium \((Q_1^*, P_1^*)\). When both curves shift simultaneously, one outcome variable moves unambiguously while the other becomes ambiguous unless we know which shift is larger. Table~\(\ref{tab:comparative_statics}\) summarizes all eight single and simultaneous shift cases.


Visual Representation
Figure 3 shows initial equilibrium \(E_1^*(20, \$60)\), the surplus at a price of \(\$80\), and the new equilibrium \(E_2^*(25, \$70)\) following a rightward demand shift.



Figure 3. Market Equilibrium and Demand Shift. At \(\$80\), the original curves imply \(Q_d=10\) and \(Q_s=30\), a surplus of \(20\) units. A rightward shift in demand creates a shortage at the original equilibrium price of \(\$60\); the market moves to \(E_2^*(25,\$70)\).




Real-World Application: Simultaneous Shifts and Coffee Prices
As a hypothetical, suppose greater demand for AI servers shifts semiconductor demand right while new fabrication capacity shifts supply right. Both shifts raise equilibrium quantity; their effects on equilibrium price oppose one another, so the net price change depends on the relative sizes of the shifts.
FRED’s series APU0000717311 reports an average U.S. city price for a pound of 100% ground-roast coffee; its July 2026 observation is \(\$9.317\) per pound, not seasonally adjusted. This is a single-product market price observation—not a measure of quantity, not a way to identify a demand or supply shift by itself, and not an economy-wide inflation index. FRED cautions that average-price series are best for the price in a particular month; economists use aggregate price indexes (such as the CPI, PPI, or GDP Deflator, covered in Macroeconomics) to study economy-wide price changes over time.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Market equilibrium solves the system of two linear equations simultaneously (assuming linear demand and supply with nonnegative quantities):
\[
Q_d(P^*) = Q_s(P^*) \quad \text{or} \quad P_d(Q^*) = P_s(Q^*)
\]






NoteWork It Out: Market Equilibrium, Disequilibrium, and Comparative Statics



In a city’s market for portable solar generators, demand is \(Q_d = 500 - 2P\) and supply is \(Q_s = -100 + 4P\) (for \(P \ge \$25\)).

Solve for the initial market equilibrium price \(P_1^*\) and quantity \(Q_1^*\).
Determine whether a price of \(P = \$120\) creates a surplus or a shortage, and compute its exact size.
Suppose lower solar-cell costs shift supply rightward by \(60\) generators at every price, giving \(Q_s^{\text{new}} = -40 + 4P\) (for \(P \ge \$10\)). Find the new equilibrium \((Q_2^*, P_2^*)\) and verify the comparative statics prediction.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Set \(Q_d = Q_s\) and Solve for \(P_1^*\):

\[
500 - 2P_1^* = -100 + 4P_1^* \implies 600 = 6P_1^* \implies P_1^* = \mathbf{\$100}
\]
Substitute \(P_1^* = \$100\) into either equation to find \(Q_1^*\):
\[
Q_1^* = 500 - 2(100) = \mathbf{300\text{ generators}} \qquad (\text{check: } -100 + 4(100) = 300)
\]

Evaluate Disequilibrium at \(P = \$120\):

\[
Q_d(120) = 500 - 2(120) = 260\text{ units}, \qquad Q_s(120) = -100 + 4(120) = 380\text{ units}
\]
Because \(Q_s\ (380) > Q_d\ (260)\), there is a surplus of \(380 - 260 = \mathbf{120\text{ generators}}\).

Solve the Shifted Equilibrium (\(Q_d = Q_s^{\text{new}}\)):

\[
500 - 2P_2^* = -40 + 4P_2^* \implies 540 = 6P_2^* \implies P_2^* = \mathbf{\$90}
\]
Substitute \(P_2^* = \$90\) into either equation:
\[
Q_2^* = 500 - 2(90) = \mathbf{320\text{ generators}} \qquad (\text{check: } -40 + 4(90) = 320)
\]
Conclusion: The initial market clears at \(P_1^* = \$100\) and \(Q_1^* = 300\); pricing above equilibrium at \(\$120\) leaves \(120\) unsold units on shelves. When lower input costs shift supply rightward by \(60\) units, equilibrium price falls from \(\$100\) to \(\$90\) and equilibrium quantity rises from \(300\) to \(320\)—matching Table~\(\ref{tab:comparative_statics}\).








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Comparative Statics via Total Differentiation



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Let general demand be \(Q_d(P, \alpha)\) with \(\frac{\partial Q_d}{\partial P} < 0\) and shift parameter \(\alpha\) (\(\frac{\partial Q_d}{\partial \alpha} > 0\)), and let upward-sloping supply be \(Q_s(P)\) with \(\frac{dQ_s}{dP} > 0\). Differentiating the equilibrium identity \(Q_d(P^*, \alpha) - Q_s(P^*) = 0\) with respect to \(\alpha\):
\[
\frac{\partial Q_d}{\partial P} \frac{dP^*}{d\alpha} + \frac{\partial Q_d}{\partial \alpha} - \frac{dQ_s}{dP}\frac{dP^*}{d\alpha} = 0 \implies \frac{dP^*}{d\alpha} = \frac{\partial Q_d / \partial \alpha}{\frac{dQ_s}{dP} - \frac{\partial Q_d}{\partial P}} > 0
\]
Because \(\frac{dQ_s}{dP} > 0\) and \(\frac{\partial Q_d}{\partial P} < 0\), the denominator is strictly positive, confirming analytically that any positive demand shock (\(\partial Q_d / \partial \alpha > 0\)) strictly raises equilibrium price \(P^*\) and equilibrium quantity (\(\frac{dQ^*}{d\alpha} = \frac{dQ_s}{dP}\frac{dP^*}{d\alpha} > 0\)).








TipBring It Home: Diagnosing the Campus Coffee Market



Return to the campus coffee shop from the start of the chapter. If the shop raised its menu price and sold fewer lattes while no outside market factor changed, students simply moved upward along the existing demand curve (a lower quantity demanded). If a rival café opened nearby, student demand for the original shop shifted leftward, pushing both equilibrium price and quantity down. If coffee-bean costs jumped, supply shifted leftward, pushing price up and quantity down. And if student demand rose during finals week at the same time bean costs rose, Table~\(\ref{tab:comparative_statics}\) shows that equilibrium price must rise while the net change in quantity depends on which shift is larger. In every case, \(P\) refers specifically to the single-market price of campus coffee—distinct from economy-wide inflation indexes.

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
section: Practice Questions
text:
Practice Questions

Demand is \(Q_d=400-10P\). At \(P=\$15\), demand then rises by 80 subscriptions at every price. What is the new quantity demanded?



Incorrect: This is the original quantity at \(P=\$15\) and ignores the demand shift.


Incorrect: This subtracts 80 instead of adding the stated increase.


Correct: The original quantity is \(400-10(15)=250\); after the shift it is \(250+80=330\).


Incorrect: This is the new demand intercept, not quantity at \(P=\$15\).



Original supply is \(Q_s=-40+8P\) for \(P\ge\$5\). Input costs raise the minimum acceptable price by \(\$3\) per loaf. At \(P=\$10\), what quantity is supplied under the new curve?


40 loaves. Incorrect: This uses the original curve, \(-40+8(10)\).
24 loaves. Incorrect: This is the reduction in supply at \(\$10\), not the new quantity supplied.
16 loaves. Correct: The shifted curve is \(Q_s=-64+8P\), so \(Q_s=-64+80=16\).
8 loaves. Incorrect: This confuses the new minimum price with quantity supplied.


Demand is \(Q_d=500-2P\) and supply is \(Q_s=-100+4P\). At \(P=\$120\), what is the disequilibrium?


A shortage of 120 generators. Incorrect: It reverses which quantity is larger.
A surplus of 120 generators. Correct: \(Q_d=260\) and \(Q_s=380\), so the surplus is \(380-260=120\).
A surplus of 80 generators. Incorrect: It subtracts the equilibrium quantity, 300, from one disequilibrium quantity.
No disequilibrium. Incorrect: \(P=\$120\) is above the equilibrium price of \(\$100\).


Demand and supply both shift right. Which conclusion follows under the standard upward-sloping supply and downward-sloping demand model?


Equilibrium price and quantity both rise. Incorrect: The demand shift raises price, but the supply shift lowers it.
Equilibrium price and quantity both fall. Incorrect: Both shifts increase equilibrium quantity.
Equilibrium quantity rises; the price change is ambiguous. Correct: Both shifts raise quantity, while their opposing effects on price require knowing relative shift sizes.
Equilibrium quantity is ambiguous; price must fall. Incorrect: It reverses the unambiguous quantity result and overstates the price effect.

title: 4  Chapter 4: Consumer and Producer Surplus, Market Efficiency, and Welfare
text: 4.1 Consumer Surplus and Marginal Willingness to Pay
crumbs: 4  Chapter 4: Consumer and Producer Surplus, Market Efficiency, and Welfare

title: 4  Chapter 4: Consumer and Producer Surplus, Market Efficiency, and Welfare
text:
1. Conceptual Introduction
Have you ever walked into a store prepared to spend \(\$50\) on a pair of shoes, only to find them on sale for \(\$30\)? If so, you walked out with the shoes and an extra \(\$20\) in your pocket that you were completely willing to part with. In economics, that \(\$20\) gain is called your Consumer Surplus (\(CS\)). Every shopper enters the market with a personal maximum price in mind—the highest dollar amount they would pay before walking away empty-handed. Economists call this boundary your willingness to pay (WTP). Whenever the actual market price is lower than what you were willing to pay, you capture a net financial and psychological win.
In a market, buyers purchase goods one unit at a time. The very first buyers—or the first few items purchased—usually have the highest personal value to consumers (what economists sometimes call ``early buyers’’ or intramarginal units). For instance, your first cup of coffee in the morning might be worth \(\$8\) to you, but the café only charges \(\$4\), giving you \(\$4\) in surplus. Your second cup might be worth \(\$5\), giving you \(\$1\) in surplus. By the time you consider a third cup, its value to you might drop to exactly \(\$4\). For that final unit, your willingness to pay matches the market price, yielding zero extra surplus. If price rose to \(\$4.01\), you simply would not buy it.
When we add up the surplus enjoyed by every single customer in the entire market, we get Total Consumer Surplus. It represents the total dollar value of happiness, savings, and satisfaction that consumers walk away with over and above what they had to pay. When prices drop—thanks to new technology, cheaper shipping, or increased competition—consumer surplus expands, leaving households with more money left over to spend on other goals like tuition, healthcare, or savings.


2. Visual Representation
Figure 1 graphs consumer surplus on a standard market diagram.






NoteGraphing Tip: Why is Price on the Vertical Y-Axis?



In high school algebra, you usually put the independent variable on the horizontal \(x\)-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical \(y\)-axis (\(y = f(x)\)). In economics, by historical tradition dating back to Alfred Marshall in 1890, we place Price (\(P\)) on the vertical axis and Quantity (\(Q\)) on the horizontal axis. When looking at a demand equation like \(P = 100 - 2Q\), to find the top vertical intercept (the choke price where nobody buys anything), simply plug in \(Q = 0\), giving \(P = \$100\).





Figure 1. Consumer Surplus on the Linear Demand Plane. Consumer surplus is the shaded blue triangle located below the demand curve and above the \(\$60\) market price line.




3. Real-World Application: Airline Dynamic Pricing and Flight Upgrades
Imagine a college student flying home for Thanksgiving break versus a business consultant booking a flight to close a critical \(\$100,000\) client deal.

The consultant has an urgent deadline. Their company’s maximum willingness to pay for a last-minute seat is $900.
The student has a tight budget. Their personal maximum willingness to pay is $400.

When both go online, the airline lists the standard coach fare at $350. Both travelers buy a ticket at that exact price, but look at the difference in their net surplus:
\[
\text{Consultant's Surplus} = \$900 - \$350 = \mathbf{\$550}
\]
\[
\text{Student's Surplus} = \$400 - \$350 = \mathbf{\$50}
\]
Both sit in identical seats drinking the same tomato juice, but the consultant captures \(\$550\) in surplus while the student captures \(\$50\). This real-world difference explains why airlines work so hard with algorithms to separate travelers and charge higher fares to business passengers whenever possible.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Because the demand curve in our example is a straight line, the area of Consumer Surplus forms a simple right-angled triangle. You do not need any advanced calculus—just basic high school geometry:
\[
\text{Consumer Surplus } (CS) = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Base} \times \text{Height}
\]
Where:

\(\text{Base} = Q^*\) (The quantity of units bought at the market price).
\(\text{Height} = P_{\text{choke}} - P^*\) (The vertical gap between the highest walk-away price on the demand curve and the actual price paid).

Worked Problem: A campus bookstore sells portable battery chargers according to the demand equation:
\[
P = 100 - 2Q
\]
If the market price settles at \(P^* = \$60\), calculate the total Consumer Surplus enjoyed by students.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Find the Choke Price (\(P_{\text{choke}}\)): The choke price is the vertical intercept where quantity demanded drops to zero (\(Q = 0\)). Plug \(0\) in for \(Q\):

\[
P_{\text{choke}} = 100 - 2(0) = \$100
\]
Meaning: If the store charged \(\$100\) or more, zero students would buy a charger.

Solve for the Quantity Bought (\(Q^*\)): Plug the market price of \(\$60\) into the demand equation and solve for \(Q\):

\[
60 = 100 - 2Q
\]
Subtract \(100\) from both sides:
\[
-40 = -2Q
\]
Divide both sides by \(-2\):
\[
Q^* = 20\text{ chargers}
\]
Meaning: At a price of \(\$60\), students purchase 20 chargers.

Find the Height of the Surplus Triangle:

\[
\text{Height} = P_{\text{choke}} - P^* = \$100 - \$60 = \$40
\]

Calculate the Area of the Consumer Surplus Triangle:

\[
CS = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Base} \times \text{Height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times \$40 = 10 \times \$40 = \mathbf{\$400}
\]
Conclusion: Students receive a total net economic benefit of $400 beyond what they paid for the chargers.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus Extension



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: When demand curves are curved rather than straight lines (\(P = P(q)\)), the area is found by taking the definite integral of marginal willingness to pay minus the market price from 0 to \(Q^*\):
\[
CS = \int_{0}^{Q^*} \left[ P(q) - P^* \right] dq
\]
For our linear equation \(P(q) = 100 - 2q\) with \(Q^* = 20\) and \(P^* = 60\):
\[
CS = \int_{0}^{20} (100 - 2q - 60)\,dq = \int_{0}^{20} (40 - 2q)\,dq = \left[ 40q - q^2 \right]_{0}^{20} = (40(20) - 20^2) - 0 = 800 - 400 = \mathbf{\$400}
\]
Notice that elementary triangle geometry and calculus yield the exact same \(\$400\) result.

title: 4  Chapter 4: Consumer and Producer Surplus, Market Efficiency, and Welfare
section: 4.2 Producer Surplus and Marginal Cost
text:
4.2 Producer Surplus and Marginal Cost

1. Conceptual Introduction
Just as consumers gain surplus by paying less than their maximum valuation, sellers gain surplus by selling goods for more than it cost to make them. Every business owner has a minimum price they must receive before they agree to produce and sell an additional unit. Economists call this threshold their willingness to accept (WTA), which directly equals the marginal cost (\(MC\)) of producing that extra item.
Producer Surplus (\(PS\)) is the net operating gain earned by firms. It is the gap between the money a firm collects at the market price and the minimum cost required to produce those items:
\[
PS = \text{Total Revenue Received} - \text{Total Variable Cost of Production}
\]
A vital point for business and economics students is that producer surplus is not the same thing as total accounting profit. Profit subtracts all costs, including fixed overhead like building rent, machinery leases, and insurance (\(\text{Profit} = \text{Revenue} - \text{Variable Costs} - \text{Fixed Costs}\)). Producer surplus only looks at operating revenue minus the direct, day-to-day variable costs of making the product (\(PS = \text{Revenue} - \text{Variable Costs}\)). That operating surplus is the cash flow a firm uses to pay its fixed rent and earn an eventual profit.
Because supply curves slope upward (due to diminishing returns and rising production costs), earlier units can be produced very cheaply, generating large operating surplus. The very last unit produced breaks even on operating costs (\(P^* = MC\)).


2. Visual Representation
Figure 2 depicts Producer Surplus as the red shaded triangle located above the supply curve and below the market price line.



Figure 2. Producer Surplus on the Linear Supply Plane. Producer surplus is the shaded red triangle located above the supply curve and below the \(\$60\) market price line.




3. Real-World Application: Coffee Shops and Morning Espresso Sales
Consider an independent café in San Francisco selling cold brew coffee for $5.00 a cup.

The direct variable cost (coffee beans, filtered water, compostable cup, and milk) for the barista to brew the first batch of cups is only about $1.50 per cup.
On those early cups, the coffee shop earns a producer surplus of:

\[
\text{Surplus per Cup} = \$5.00 - \$1.50 = \mathbf{\$3.50}
\]
As the morning rush peaks, the café has to hire extra staff and run grinders continuously at higher overtime expense, pushing the marginal cost of the 300th cup up to $4.50. Even on that late cup, the café still captures \(\$0.50\) in surplus.
Across 300 cups, the accumulated producer surplus might total \(\$600\) for the morning. Does the owner pocket all \(\$600\) as pure profit? No—they must use that \(\$600\) producer surplus to pay fixed bills like the \(\$4,000\) monthly shop rent, electric utilities, and insurance. Whatever is left over after paying fixed costs is their economic profit.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
For a linear supply curve, Producer Surplus (\(PS\)) is calculated as the area of a right-angled triangle:
\[
\text{Producer Surplus } (PS) = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Base} \times \text{Height}
\]
Where:

\(\text{Base} = Q^*\) (The quantity sold in the market).
\(\text{Height} = P^* - P_{\text{min}}\) (The difference between the market price received and the minimum threshold price at the bottom of the supply curve).

Worked Problem: A group of student tutoring services has an aggregate supply curve given by:
\[
P = 20 + 2Q
\]
If the equilibrium tutoring wage settles at \(P^* = \$60\) per session, compute the total Producer Surplus earned by the student tutors.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Find the Minimum Supply Price (\(P_{\text{min}}\)): Plug \(Q = 0\) into the supply curve:

\[
P_{\text{min}} = 20 + 2(0) = \$20
\]
Meaning: Below \(\$20\), no tutor is willing to work a session.

Solve for the Quantity Supplied (\(Q^*\)): Set the market price equal to the supply equation:

\[
60 = 20 + 2Q \implies 40 = 2Q \implies Q^* = 20\text{ sessions}
\]

Calculate the Height of the Triangle:

\[
\text{Height} = P^* - P_{\text{min}} = \$60 - \$20 = \$40
\]

Compute the Total Producer Surplus Area:

\[
PS = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Base} \times \text{Height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times \$40 = 10 \times \$40 = \mathbf{\$400}
\]
Conclusion: The student tutors earn a collective operating surplus of $400 above their minimum hourly opportunity costs.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus Extension



Note for Economics Majors: For continuous, non-linear marginal cost curves \(MC(q)\), Producer Surplus is the integral of the market price minus marginal cost from 0 to \(Q^*\):
\[
PS = \int_{0}^{Q^*} \left[ P^* - MC(q) \right] dq = \int_{0}^{20} (60 - (20 + 2q))\,dq = \int_{0}^{20} (40 - 2q)\,dq = \left[ 40q - q^2 \right]_{0}^{20} = \mathbf{\$400}
\]

title: 4  Chapter 4: Consumer and Producer Surplus, Market Efficiency, and Welfare
section: 4.3 Allocative Efficiency and Price Controls
text:
4.3 Allocative Efficiency and Price Controls

1. Conceptual Introduction
When we combine both sides of the market, we arrive at the total economic gain created by voluntary trade, known as Total Social Surplus (\(TS\)):
\[
\text{Total Social Surplus} = \text{Consumer Surplus} + \text{Producer Surplus}
\]
Notice something remarkable about this equation: the market price itself actually cancels out! Price simply determines how the economic pie is divided between buyers and sellers. If the price goes up, buyers get less surplus and sellers get more; if the price goes down, buyers get more and sellers get less. But the overall size of the pie depends entirely on how many mutually beneficial trades are allowed to happen.
A competitive market in equilibrium achieves what economists call allocative efficiency. At the point where the supply and demand curves cross, the marginal benefit to society matches the marginal cost of producing the good (\(MB = MC\)). Every buyer who values the good at more than it costs to make gets one, and no resources are wasted making products that people don’t value. Economists call this condition Pareto efficiency: at this exact output level, you cannot make one person better off without making someone else worse off.
When governments try to dictate prices by law—such as imposing a legal maximum price (price ceiling)—the market cannot reach this balance. If the ceiling is set below the natural equilibrium price, two things happen: sellers produce fewer units because low prices do not cover their costs, while buyers rush to purchase more because it is cheap. This creates an immediate physical shortage. More importantly, trades that both buyers and sellers wanted to make are legally blocked, shrinking the total economic pie and creating a permanent loss to society called deadweight loss.


2. Visual Representation
Figure 3 shows the market in natural balance, maximizing the total economic pie to \(\$800\). Figure 4 shows what happens when the government imposes a price ceiling at \(\$40\).



Figure 3. Maximized Social Surplus in a Free Market. At equilibrium \(E^*(20, \$60)\), Total Social Surplus is \(\$400 + \$400 = \$800\), and no trades are wasted.





Figure 4. The Impact of a Binding Price Ceiling. Capping the price at \(\$40\) causes quantity supplied to collapse to \(10\) while quantity demanded jumps to \(30\), creating a shortage of \(20\) units and an orange Deadweight Loss triangle of lost trades.




3. Real-World Application: Rent Control in San Francisco and New York
In expensive housing markets like San Francisco and New York City, local governments often cap how much landlords can raise apartment rents each year. The compassionate goal is simple: keep current residents from being priced out of their neighborhoods.
However, consider the economic consequences over time:

Supply Collapses: Landlords faced with capped rents cannot cover rising maintenance, plumbing, and property tax costs. Some convert apartments into luxury condos, while developers stop building modest rental apartments altogether.
Demand Surges: Low capped rents encourage people to stay in huge apartments alone or move in from outside the city.
The Result: A severe housing shortage. College students and young workers searching for an apartment face lines around the block, application lotteries, and expensive broker finder fees. While incumbent tenants lucky enough to have a rent-controlled lease benefit, many others are locked out completely—an exact demonstration of deadweight loss and shortages in action.



4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Let’s analyze the exact numbers when the government imposes a price ceiling of \(\bar{P} = \$40\) on our battery charger market (\(P_d = 100 - 2Q\) and \(P_s = 20 + 2Q\)).
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Calculate Quantity Supplied (\(Q_s\)) under the Ceiling: Plug \(P = \$40\) into the supply equation:

\[
40 = 20 + 2Q_s \implies 20 = 2Q_s \implies Q_s = \mathbf{10\text{ units}}
\]
Result: Sellers only produce 10 chargers because \(\$40\) barely covers their costs.

Calculate Quantity Demanded (\(Q_d\)) under the Ceiling: Plug \(P = \$40\) into the demand equation:

\[
40 = 100 - 2Q_d \implies 2Q_d = 60 \implies Q_d = \mathbf{30\text{ units}}
\]
Result: At the bargain price of \(\$40\), students line up wanting 30 chargers.

Calculate the Physical Shortage:

\[
\text{Shortage} = Q_d - Q_s = 30 - 10 = \mathbf{20\text{ units}}
\]

Identify the Actual Number of Transactions: Because it takes two willing parties to make a deal, the number of units actually bought and sold is limited by whoever produces the least:

\[
Q_{\text{actual}} = \min(Q_s, Q_d) = \min(10, 30) = \mathbf{10\text{ units}}
\]

Calculate the Value of the 10th Unit to Consumers: What was the 10th charger worth to students? Plug \(Q = 10\) into the demand curve:

\[
P = 100 - 2(10) = \$80
\]

Calculate Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)): The market dropped from producing 20 units down to 10 units. Trades for units 11 through 20 were completely eliminated. The lost value forms the orange triangle in Figure 4:

\[
\text{Base of DWL Triangle} = \text{Vertical Gap at } Q=10 = \$80 - \$40 = \$40
\]
\[
\text{Height of DWL Triangle} = Q^* - Q_s = 20 - 10 = 10\text{ units}
\]
\[
DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Base} \times \text{Height} = \frac{1}{2} \times \$40 \times 10 = \mathbf{\$200}
\]
Conclusion: The price ceiling destroyed $200 in social surplus that both students and producers would have shared if trade had not been blocked.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Social Planner Maximization



Note for Economics Majors: A benevolent social planner chooses total output \(Q\) to maximize total surplus:
\[
\max_Q W(Q) = \int_{0}^{Q} \left[ P_d(q) - P_s(q) \right] dq
\]
Taking the first derivative with respect to \(Q\) and setting it to 0:
\[
\frac{dW}{dQ} = P_d(Q) - P_s(Q) = 0 \implies P_d(Q^*) = P_s(Q^*)
\]
This proves mathematically that social welfare is strictly maximized where supply meets demand. Any artificial intervention that forces \(Q \neq Q^*\) mathematically guarantees \(W(Q) < W(Q^*)\).
