title: 6  Chapter 6: The Theory of the Firm: Production and Cost Curves
section: 6.2 Short-Run Cost Structure and Curve Geometry
text:
6.2 Short-Run Cost Structure and Curve Geometry

1. Conceptual Introduction
Every physical production schedule has a direct mirror image in dollar costs. In the short run, a firm’s Total Cost (\(TC\)) splits into two categories:

Fixed Costs (\(FC\)): Overhead expenses that do not vary with output level—such as building rent, equipment leases, and property insurance. Even if the firm produces \(Q = 0\), it still pays \(FC\).
Variable Costs (\(VC\)): Expenses that rise as output increases—such as hourly wages, raw ingredients, and shipping boxes. At \(Q = 0\), \(VC = 0\).

Dividing total costs by output \(Q\) gives per-unit average costs: Average Fixed Cost (\(AFC = FC/Q\)), which falls continuously as overhead is spread over more units, Average Variable Cost (\(AVC = VC/Q\)), and Average Total Cost (\(ATC = TC/Q = AFC + AVC\)).
The single most important cost metric for pricing and output decisions is Marginal Cost (\(MC = \Delta TC / \Delta Q\))—the extra cost of producing one additional unit. Because fixed costs do not change when \(Q\) increases, marginal cost is driven entirely by variable inputs and is inversely linked to worker productivity (\(MC = w / MP_L\), where \(w\) is the wage rate). When diminishing marginal product sets in (\(MP_L \downarrow\)), marginal cost rises (\(MC \uparrow\)), giving \(MC\), \(AVC\), and \(ATC\) their classic U-shapes.


2. Visual Representation
Figure 2 illustrates the canonical geometry of short-run cost curves, highlighting how \(MC\) intersects both \(AVC\) and \(ATC\) at their exact minimum points.






NoteClear It Up: Why MC Crosses ATC and AVC at Their Minimums (By Design)



Think of your cumulative GPA. If your GPA is \(3.40\) and you earn a \(3.80\) in your next class (your marginal grade), your cumulative GPA gets pulled upward. If you earn a \(2.90\), your cumulative GPA gets pulled downward. Cost curves obey the exact same arithmetic: whenever \(MC < ATC\), the next unit is cheaper than the average and pulls \(ATC\) down; whenever \(MC > ATC\), the next unit is more expensive and pulls \(ATC\) up. Therefore, \(MC\) must cross \(ATC\) (and \(AVC\)) at its exact lowest point!





Figure 2. Short-Run Per-Unit Cost Curves. Average Fixed Cost (\(AFC\)) declines steadily as output expands. Marginal Cost (\(MC\)) slopes upward due to diminishing returns and intersects both \(AVC\) and \(ATC\) at their respective minimum points.




3. Real-World Application: Fixed Overhead vs. Variable Costs in Commercial Aviation
Operating a commercial jetliner involves massive fixed costs—aircraft lease payments, hangar maintenance, and pilot salaries—that must be paid whether a plane carries \(40\) passengers or \(180\) passengers. As an airline fills more seats on a route, its Average Fixed Cost per passenger drops sharply, pulling Average Total Cost downward. The airline reaches MES—the most efficient scale for that aircraft type—when it fills most of its available seats, balancing the fixed overhead against variable operating costs per flight.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
The core short-run cost identities are:
\[
TC = FC + VC, \qquad ATC = \frac{TC}{Q} = AFC + AVC, \qquad MC = \frac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q} = \frac{\Delta VC}{\Delta Q}
\]
Worked Problem: A custom bakery has daily fixed rent and oven lease costs of \(FC = \$200\). Its total variable costs for baking batches of artisan sourdough loaves (\(Q\)) are:

\(Q = 0 \implies VC = \$0\)
\(Q = 10 \implies VC = \$100\)
\(Q = 20 \implies VC = \$180\)
\(Q = 30 \implies VC = \$310\)

Calculate \(TC\), \(AFC\), \(AVC\), \(ATC\), and \(MC\) at \(Q = 20\) and \(Q = 30\) loaves.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute Costs at \(Q = 20\):

\[
TC_{20} = \$200 + \$180 = \mathbf{\$380}
\]
\[
AFC_{20} = \frac{\$200}{20} = \mathbf{\$10.00}, \qquad AVC_{20} = \frac{\$180}{20} = \mathbf{\$9.00}, \qquad ATC_{20} = \frac{\$380}{20} = \mathbf{\$19.00}
\]
\[
MC_{10 \to 20} = \frac{\$380 - \$300}{20 - 10} = \frac{\$80}{10} = \mathbf{\$8.00\text{ per loaf}}
\]

Compute Costs at \(Q = 30\):

\[
TC_{30} = \$200 + \$310 = \mathbf{\$510}
\]
\[
AFC_{30} = \frac{\$200}{30} \approx \mathbf{\$6.67}, \qquad AVC_{30} = \frac{\$310}{30} \approx \mathbf{\$10.33}, \qquad ATC_{30} = \frac{\$510}{30} = \mathbf{\$17.00}
\]
\[
MC_{20 \to 30} = \frac{\$510 - \$380}{30 - 20} = \frac{\$130}{10} = \mathbf{\$13.00\text{ per loaf}}
\]
Conclusion: Between \(20\) and \(30\) loaves, \(MC = \$13.00\) is still below \(ATC_{20} = \$19.00\), so \(ATC\) continues falling from \(\$19.00\) down to \(\$17.00\).






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus Proof of Minimum Cost Crossings



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Given a differentiable Total Cost function \(TC(Q)\), Average Total Cost is \(ATC(Q) = \frac{TC(Q)}{Q}\). Differentiating \(ATC(Q)\) with respect to \(Q\) via the quotient rule yields:
\[
\frac{d(ATC)}{dQ} = \frac{Q \cdot \frac{d(TC)}{dQ} - TC(Q) \cdot 1}{Q^2} = \frac{MC(Q) - ATC(Q)}{Q}
\]
Setting \(\frac{d(ATC)}{dQ} = 0\) proves that \(ATC\) achieves its critical minimum at the exact output where \(MC(Q) = ATC(Q)\).

section: 6.3 Long-Run Costs, Economies of Scale, and Efficient Scale
text:
6.3 Long-Run Costs, Economies of Scale, and Efficient Scale

1. Conceptual Introduction
In the long run, a firm is no longer trapped inside a cramped kitchen or a single factory—it can choose among many possible plant sizes, each with its own short-run \(ATC\) curve. Consider three representative cases: a small sandwich shop, a medium regional bakery chain, and a large metropolitan production facility, each with its own short-run \(ATC\) curve. Tracing the lowest achievable per-unit cost at every output level forms the Long-Run Average Total Cost (\(LRATC\)) envelope curve by selecting the cheapest plant size for each quantity.
As a company scales up its long-run production capacity, \(LRATC\) typically passes through three distinct phases:

Economies of Scale (\(LRATC\) Slopes Downward): Doubling all inputs more than doubles output, driving per-unit costs down through worker specialization, bulk input discounts, and automated machinery.
Constant Returns to Scale (\(LRATC\) Is Flat): The firm reaches Minimum Efficient Scale (\(Q_{\text{MES}}\))—the smallest output at which \(LRATC\) reaches its lowest point. Beyond this scale, the firm experiences neither further cost savings nor rising costs, until diseconomies eventually appear.
Diseconomies of Scale (\(LRATC\) Slopes Upward): Beyond a massive size, bureaucracy, communication breakdowns, and managerial bloat cause per-unit costs to rise again.



2. Visual Representation
Figure 3 shows the U-shaped Long-Run Average Total Cost (\(LRATC\)) curve enveloping three short-run plant sizes (\(SRATC_1\), \(SRATC_2\), and \(SRATC_3\)).



Figure 3. Long-Run Average Total Cost (\(LRATC\)). Expanding from a small plant to a medium plant captures economies of scale until reaching Minimum Efficient Scale (\(Q_{\text{MES}}\)), after which excessive size generates diseconomies of scale.




3. Real-World Application: Semiconductor Fabs vs. Local Coffee Shops
Modern semiconductor fabrication plants cost over \(\$15\text{ billion}\) to construct, meaning \(LRATC\) falls steeply over millions of wafers—creating massive economies of scale that explain why only a handful of global firms (such as TSMC, Samsung, and Intel) manufacture leading-edge chips. By contrast, independent coffee shops reach Minimum Efficient Scale at a very modest daily volume, allowing hundreds of small cafés to coexist competitively across a single city.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Long-run returns to scale compare the percentage increase in output (\(\%\Delta Q\)) to a proportional percentage increase in all inputs (\(\%\Delta \text{Inputs}\)):
\[
\text{Economies of Scale} \iff \%\Delta Q > \%\Delta \text{Inputs} \iff LRATC \downarrow
\]
Worked Problem: A regional solar-panel manufacturer doubles all of its factory floor space, assembly robots, and technicians (\(+100\%\) increase in all inputs). Its annual output rises from \(50{,}000\) panels to \(125{,}000\) panels, while total long-run cost doubles from \(\$10{,}000{,}000\) to \(\$20{,}000{,}000\). Compute \(LRATC\) before and after expansion and identify the scale regime.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute Initial \(LRATC_1\):

\[
LRATC_1 = \frac{\$10{,}000{,}000}{50{,}000} = \mathbf{\$200\text{ per panel}}
\]

Compute Expanded \(LRATC_2\):

\[
LRATC_2 = \frac{\$20{,}000{,}000}{125{,}000} = \mathbf{\$160\text{ per panel}}
\]

Compare Input Growth vs. Output Growth: Inputs increased by \(100\%\), while output increased by \(\frac{125{,}000 - 50{,}000}{50{,}000} = +150\%\).

Conclusion: Because output grew faster than inputs (\(150\% > 100\%\)) and per-unit cost fell from \(\$200\) to \(\$160\), the firm is experiencing economies of scale.

title: 7  Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium
text:
Conceptual Introduction
Imagine a family corn farm in Iowa ready to sell its autumn harvest at a local grain elevator. Even if the farm harvests tens of thousands of bushels, it represents a microscopic share of global grain production and cannot negotiate its own price—it sells at the prevailing commodity spot price. Economists model markets like this using perfect competition, an idealized benchmark defined by four strict assumptions: (1) many small buyers and sellers, (2) identical (homogeneous) products across every firm, (3) perfect information about prices and quality, and (4) free entry and exit in the long run with zero barriers. Agricultural commodities such as wheat, corn, and soybeans come closest to this benchmark in practice.
Because each competitive firm supplies a tiny fraction of total market output and sells an identical product, an individual producer has zero power to raise price above the going market rate—if a farmer charges even one penny more, buyers switch instantly to neighboring sellers. Conversely, there is no reason to cut price below the market rate because the firm can already sell all it wishes at the going price. Consequently, every competitive firm is a price taker facing a perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand curve at the market equilibrium price \(P^*\). Every additional unit sold adds exactly \(P^*\) to Total Revenue (\(TR = P^* \times q\)), meaning Price equals Marginal Revenue and Average Revenue (\(P^* = MR = AR\)).
To maximize economic profit (\(\pi = TR - TC\)), a competitive firm expands output one unit at a time as long as the extra revenue from selling another unit exceeds the extra cost of producing it (\(MR > MC\)). It stops at the exact quantity \(q^*\) where Marginal Revenue equals Marginal Cost on the upward-sloping portion of the \(MC\) curve:
\[
P^* = MR = MC(q^*)
\]
Once optimal output \(q^*\) is chosen, the firm’s profit or loss per unit is the vertical gap between market price \(P^*\) and Average Total Cost (\(ATC\)) at \(q^*\), giving total economic profit \(\pi = (P^* - ATC) \times q^*\). When global grain prices surge due to droughts elsewhere, an individual farmer’s horizontal \(P = MR\) line shifts upward, prompting the farmer to apply extra inputs and expand output along \(MC\) to capture positive short-run economic profits.






NoteClear It Up: Market Demand Slopes Down, Yet the Firm’s Demand Is Horizontal



Students often wonder how market demand can obey the Law of Demand (sloping downward) while each competitive firm faces a flat demand curve. The resolution is scale: in the entire market, lower prices are required to persuade consumers to buy millions of extra bushels. For a single small farm, however, expanding output from \(50\) to \(100\) bushels is a drop in the ocean—too small to move the market price noticeably—so the individual firm takes \(P^*\) as fixed.




Visual Representation
Figure 1 links the overall industry supply-and-demand equilibrium (left) to an individual price-taking firm earning positive short-run economic profit (right).



Figure 1. Short-Run Profit Maximization under Perfect Competition. Market supply and demand set equilibrium price \(P^*\) (left), giving the individual price-taking firm a horizontal \(P^* = MR\) line (right). Producing \(q^*\) where \(P^* = MC\) yields positive short-run economic profit equal to the shaded teal rectangle \((P^* - ATC(q^*)) \times q^*\).




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Assuming the firm is a price taker with a rising Marginal Cost schedule and operates above its shutdown threshold (\(P^* \ge \min AVC\)), profit maximization occurs at \(P^* = MC(q^*)\), generating total economic profit:
\[
\pi = TR - TC = (P^* - ATC) \times q^*
\]






NoteWork It Out: Short-Run Profit Maximization for a Blueberry Grower



Problem: An illustrative competitive blueberry grower faces a market price of \(P^* = \$30\) per crate. The grower’s Total Cost, Average Variable Cost, and Marginal Cost schedules are:
\[
TC(q) = 48 + 6q + 2q^2, \qquad AVC(q) = 6 + 2q, \qquad MC(q) = 6 + 4q
\]
Find the profit-maximizing quantity of crates \(q^*\), Average Total Cost at \(q^*\), and total economic profit \(\pi\).
Step-by-Step Solution:

Apply the Profit-Maximization Rule (\(P^* = MC\)): Set market price equal to Marginal Cost and solve for \(q^*\):

\[
30 = 6 + 4q^* \implies 24 = 4q^* \implies q^* = \mathbf{6\text{ crates}}
\]
Check that the firm covers variable costs: at \(q^* = 6\), \(AVC(6) = 6 + 2(6) = \$18 < \$30\), so operating is profitable.

Calculate Total Cost (\(TC\)) and Average Total Cost (\(ATC\)) at \(q^* = 6\):

\[
TC(6) = 48 + 6(6) + 2(6^2) = 48 + 36 + 72 = \$156
\]
\[
ATC(6) = \frac{\$156}{6} = \mathbf{\$26.00\text{ per crate}}
\]

Calculate Economic Profit (\(\pi\)) Two Ways: Using Total Revenue (\(TR = \$30 \times 6 = \$180\)) minus Total Cost:

\[
\pi = TR - TC = \$180 - \$156 = \mathbf{+\$24}
\]
Cross-checking with the profit-rectangle formula:
\[
\pi = (P^* - ATC) \times q^* = (\$30 - \$26) \times 6 = \$4 \times 6 = \mathbf{+\$24}
\]
Conclusion: Producing \(6\) crates per period maximizes short-run economic profit at \(+\$24\).








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus Conditions for Profit Maximization



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: A competitive firm chooses \(q \ge 0\) to maximize \(\pi(q) = P^* q - TC(q)\). The first-order condition (FOC) requires:
\[
\frac{d\pi}{dq} = P^* - \frac{d(TC)}{dq} = P^* - MC(q) = 0 \implies P^* = MC(q^*)
\]
The second-order condition (SOC) for a local maximum requires:
\[
\frac{d^2\pi}{dq^2} = -\frac{d(MC)}{dq} < 0 \implies \frac{d(MC)}{dq} > 0
\]
Thus, profit is maximized only where \(P^* = MC\) along the upward-sloping segment of the Marginal Cost curve. For the blueberry grower above, \(TC(q) = 48 + 6q + 2q^2\) yields \(MC(q) = 6 + 4q\) and \(MC'(q) = 4 > 0\), confirming that \(q^* = 6\) is a unique global maximum.

title: 7  Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium
section: 7.2 Short-Run Shutdown vs. Long-Run Exit Rules
text:
7.2 Short-Run Shutdown vs. Long-Run Exit Rules

Conceptual Introduction
Consider an illustrative beachfront hotel in a seasonal tourist town that faces high fixed mortgage and insurance bills year-round. In November, off-peak room rates fall from \(\$280\) to \(\$95\) per night, far below the hotel’s full average cost per room. Yet the variable cost of housekeeping and utilities for an occupied room is only \(\$45\) per night. Because \(P = \$95\) exceeds \(AVC = \$45\), each occupied room contributes \(\$50\) toward paying the unavoidable mortgage, so staying open loses less money than locking the doors for the autumn.
Many students mistakenly assume that any money-losing business (\(\pi < 0\)) should immediately close. That intuition misses the crucial distinction between sunk fixed costs in the short run and escapable fixed costs in the long run:

Short-Run Shutdown Rule (\(P < \min AVC\)): In the short run, fixed costs (such as a signed building lease or property mortgage) must be paid even when output is zero. As long as market price covers Average Variable Cost (\(P \ge \min AVC\)), every unit sold pays for its workers and materials plus contributes cash toward fixed overhead. The firm should keep operating at a loss to minimize its deficit. Only when \(P < \min AVC\) does operating lose even more money than shutting down.
Long-Run Exit Rule (\(P < \min ATC\)): In the long run, leases expire and all costs become variable and avoidable. If market price remains persistently below minimum Average Total Cost (\(P < \min ATC\)), the firm cannot cover its full economic costs and will permanently exit the industry.

Consequently, a competitive firm supplies \(q = 0\) whenever \(P < \min AVC\) and produces along \(P = MC\) whenever \(P \ge \min AVC\). Therefore, the firm’s short-run supply curve is the upward-sloping portion of its Marginal Cost curve lying at or above \(\min AVC\).






NoteClear It Up: Shutdown Is Temporary; Exit Is Permanent



A shutdown is a short-run decision to produce \(q = 0\) today while remaining in the industry and still paying fixed overhead (like a ski resort closing its lifts in July while continuing to pay property taxes and loan payments). Exit is a long-run decision to leave the market permanently, terminate leases, sell equipment, and eliminate all fixed and variable costs.




Visual Representation
Figure 2 derives \(AVC\), \(ATC\), and \(MC\) from a single consistent cubic cost structure so that \(MC\) intersects both \(AVC\) and \(ATC\) at their exact mathematical minima, mapping the three short-run decision zones.



Figure 2. Short-Run Shutdown and Long-Run Exit Thresholds. Marginal Cost (\(MC\)) cuts \(AVC\) at the shutdown point \((q_{\text{SD}}, \min AVC)\) and cuts \(ATC\) at the break-even point \((q_{\text{BE}}, \min ATC)\). The firm’s short-run supply curve is the bold segment of \(MC\) above \(\min AVC\); below \(\min AVC\), the firm shuts down (\(q=0\)).




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Assuming fixed cost \(FC\) is sunk in the short run, comparing profit from operating (\(\pi_{\text{operate}} = TR - VC - FC\)) against profit from shutting down (\(\pi_{\text{shutdown}} = -FC\)) yields:
\[
\pi_{\text{operate}} \ge \pi_{\text{shutdown}} \iff TR - VC - FC \ge -FC \iff TR \ge VC \iff P \ge AVC
\]
Because a firm only chooses an interior output where \(P = MC\) on the rising segment of \(MC\), operating beats shutting down whenever \(P \ge \min AVC\).






NoteWork It Out: Short-Run Shutdown vs. Long-Run Exit for a Print Shop



Problem: An illustrative small print shop pays daily fixed rent of \(FC = \$300\). Suppose a downturn pushes the competitive market price down to \(P = \$10.00\) per print job. At its profit-maximizing (loss-minimizing) output of \(q^* = 50\) print jobs per day (where \(P = MC = \$10.00\)), its Total Variable Cost is \(VC = \$400\), so \(AVC = \$8.00\) per job and \(ATC = \$14.00\) per job. Calculate the shop’s daily loss if it operates versus its loss if it shuts down, and determine the optimal short-run and long-run decisions.
Step-by-Step Solution:

Calculate Loss If the Shop Operates (\(q^* = 50\)):

\[
TR = \$10.00 \times 50 = \$500, \qquad TC = FC + VC = \$300 + \$400 = \$700
\]
\[
\pi_{\text{operate}} = TR - TC = \$500 - \$700 = \mathbf{-\$200\text{ daily loss}}
\]

Calculate Loss If the Shop Shuts Down (\(q = 0\)): Revenue is \(\$0\) and variable cost is \(\$0\), leaving the fixed rent unpaid:

\[
\pi_{\text{shutdown}} = \$0 - \$300 = \mathbf{-\$300\text{ daily loss}}
\]

Compare Short-Run and Long-Run Thresholds: Because \(P\ (\$10.00) > AVC\ (\$8.00)\), every print job contributes \(\$2.00\) toward fixed rent, shrinking the daily loss by \(\$2.00 \times 50 = \$100\) (from \(-\$300\) to \(-\$200\)). However, because the shop still loses money even at its optimal output \(q^* = 50\) (\(P = \$10.00 < ATC = \$14.00\)), the market price necessarily lies below \(\min ATC\).

Conclusion: The shop should stay open in the short run (losing \(\$200\) instead of \(\$300\)), but exit in the long run when its lease expires unless market prices recover to at least \(\min ATC\).








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Why \(MC\) Cuts \(AVC\) and \(ATC\) at Their Minima



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Applying the quotient rule to \(AVC(q) = \frac{VC(q)}{q}\) gives:
\[
\frac{d(AVC)}{dq} = \frac{q \cdot \frac{d(VC)}{dq} - VC(q)}{q^2} = \frac{MC(q) - AVC(q)}{q}
\]
Setting \(\frac{d(AVC)}{dq} = 0\) implies \(MC(q) = AVC(q)\) at the exact minimum of \(AVC\). By the identical derivation on \(ATC(q) = \frac{TC(q)}{q}\), \(\frac{d(ATC)}{dq} = \frac{MC(q) - ATC(q)}{q} = 0\) implies \(MC(q) = ATC(q)\) at the exact minimum of \(ATC\). Hence the short-run shutdown point \((q_{\text{SD}}, \min AVC)\) and long-run break-even point \((q_{\text{BE}}, \min ATC)\) always lie on the \(MC\) curve.

title: 7  Chapter 7: Perfect Competition and Long-Run Industry Equilibrium
section: 7.3 Long-Run Industry Equilibrium and Zero Economic Profit
text:
7.3 Long-Run Industry Equilibrium and Zero Economic Profit

Conceptual Introduction
When craft breweries and gourmet food trucks surged in popularity, early operators earned substantial economic profits. Because startup barriers were modest, hundreds of new entrants opened across major cities within a few years—competing prices downward and dividing customer traffic until typical operators earned a normal return on their labor and equipment investment.
In the long run, free entry and exit act as an automatic self-correcting thermostat for perfectly competitive industries. Whenever existing firms earn positive economic profits (\(\pi > 0\)), entrepreneurs enter the market, shifting the short-run industry supply curve rightward and driving market price down until economic profits vanish. Conversely, if firms suffer economic losses (\(\pi < 0\)), producers exit when leases and equipment contracts expire, shifting industry supply leftward and pushing prices back up until remaining firms break even.
Consequently, a perfectly competitive industry settles into a long-run equilibrium characterized by the triple equality:
\[
P_{\text{LR}} = MR = MC = \min ATC
\]
At this equilibrium, firms earn zero economic profit, meaning they earn a normal accounting profit covering all explicit bills plus the owner’s full implicit opportunity cost of time and invested capital. Because each firm operates at the lowest possible average cost (\(P_{\text{LR}} = \min ATC\)) and produces the exact quantity where consumers’ marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost (\(P_{\text{LR}} = MC\)), long-run competitive equilibrium achieves both productive efficiency and allocative efficiency. In a constant-cost industry (where input prices do not change as the industry expands), the long-run industry supply curve (\(S_{\text{LR}}\)) is horizontal at \(P_{\text{LR}} = \min ATC\); in an increasing-cost industry (where expansion bids up specialized input prices), \(S_{\text{LR}}\) slopes upward, whereas in a decreasing-cost industry (where external economies lower input prices), \(S_{\text{LR}}\) slopes downward.






NoteClear It Up: Zero Economic Profit Does Not Mean Zero Accounting Profit



``Zero economic profit’’ sounds bleak only if you confuse economic profit with accounting profit. Suppose a food-truck owner earns \(\$300{,}000\) in annual revenue, pays \(\$210{,}000\) in explicit food, fuel, and permit costs, and could earn \(\$80{,}000\) managing a restaurant plus \(\$10{,}000\) in interest on invested savings. Her accounting profit is \(+\$90{,}000\), while her economic profit is \(\$90{,}000 - (\$80{,}000 + \$10{,}000) = \$0\). She is earning exactly her full opportunity cost—a healthy normal return—so she has no incentive to exit, and outsiders have no incentive to rush in.




Visual Representation
Figure 3 illustrates long-run adjustment in a constant-cost competitive industry: positive profits at \(P_1\) attract new firms, shifting industry supply from \(S_1\) to \(S_2\) until market price falls to \(P_{\text{LR}} = \min ATC\), eliminating economic profit.



Figure 3. Long-Run Competitive Equilibrium. Positive short-run profits at \(P_1\) attract new firms, shifting market supply rightward from \(S_1\) to \(S_2\) (left). Price falls until each firm’s demand line is tangent to \(\min ATC\) at \(P_{\text{LR}}\) (right), eliminating economic profit and achieving productive and allocative efficiency.




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Assuming a constant-cost industry with identical firms and free entry and exit, long-run market price equals each firm’s minimum Average Total Cost, and the equilibrium number of firms \(N^*\) divides total market demand by each firm’s efficient scale \(q_{\text{LR}}\):
\[
P_{\text{LR}} = \min ATC, \qquad N^* = \frac{Q_{\text{market}}(P_{\text{LR}})}{q_{\text{LR}}}
\]






NoteWork It Out: Long-Run Industry Equilibrium in Lawn Care



Problem: Suppose a city’s competitive lawn-care industry is a constant-cost market in which every firm has identical costs, with minimum Average Total Cost occurring at \(q_{\text{LR}} = 25\) lawns per week and \(\min ATC = \$40\) per lawn. Total weekly market demand for lawn care is linear: \(Q_d = 2{,}000 - 15P\). Find the long-run equilibrium price \(P_{\text{LR}}\), total market quantity \(Q_{\text{LR}}\), and equilibrium number of lawn-care firms \(N^*\).
Step-by-Step Solution:

Identify Long-Run Equilibrium Price (\(P_{\text{LR}}\)): Free entry and exit drive economic profit to zero, so price must equal minimum Average Total Cost:

\[
P_{\text{LR}} = \min ATC = \mathbf{\$40\text{ per lawn}}
\]

Calculate Total Market Quantity (\(Q_{\text{LR}}\)) at \(P_{\text{LR}} = \$40\): Substitute \(P_{\text{LR}} = 40\) into the market demand equation:

\[
Q_{\text{LR}} = 2{,}000 - 15(40) = 2{,}000 - 600 = \mathbf{1{,}400\text{ lawns per week}}
\]

Calculate Equilibrium Number of Firms (\(N^*\)): Divide total market output by each firm’s efficient scale (\(q_{\text{LR}} = 25\)):

\[
N^* = \frac{Q_{\text{LR}}}{q_{\text{LR}}} = \frac{1{,}400}{25} = \mathbf{56\text{ firms}}
\]
Conclusion: In long-run equilibrium, \(56\) identical firms each service \(25\) lawns per week at \(\$40\) per lawn, earning zero economic profit (a normal accounting return).








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus Derivation of Long-Run Supply



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Suppose each firm in a constant-cost competitive industry has Total Cost \(TC(q) = 100 + 20q + q^2\). Marginal Cost is \(MC(q) = \frac{d(TC)}{dq} = 20 + 2q\), and Average Total Cost is \(ATC(q) = \frac{100}{q} + 20 + q\). Setting \(MC(q) = ATC(q)\) locates minimum \(ATC\):
\[
20 + 2q = \frac{100}{q} + 20 + q \implies q = \frac{100}{q} \implies q^2 = 100 \implies q_{\text{LR}} = 10
\]
Substituting \(q_{\text{LR}} = 10\) into \(MC(q)\) (or \(ATC(q)\)) gives \(P_{\text{LR}} = 20 + 2(10) = \$40\), establishing a horizontal long-run industry supply curve at \(P_{\text{LR}} = \$40\).








TipBring It Home: Closing the Loop on the Food-Truck Market



We can now explain every puzzle from the chapter’s opening food-truck story using the three competitive rules:

Why early profits vanished: Low startup barriers allowed new trucks to enter whenever \(P > \min ATC\), shifting market supply rightward until price settled at \(P_{\text{LR}} = \min ATC\).
Why some trucks kept serving through slow winters: Truck loan payments and annual commissary leases are sunk short-run fixed costs. Any truck whose winter lunch price still exceeded its variable cost of ingredients and hourly staff (\(P \ge \min AVC\)) minimized its loss by staying open, whereas trucks with \(P < \min AVC\) shut down temporarily until spring.
Why owners stay at ``zero economic profit’’: Zero economic profit means truck owners are covering every explicit expense plus earning a full normal return on their own time and invested capital—so staying in business is just as rewarding as their next-best alternative.

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
text:
Conceptual Introduction
Imagine being the only coffee kiosk allowed inside an airport terminal after security, or the only pharmaceutical company legally permitted to manufacture a newly approved medication. At the opposite extreme from perfect competition stands a pure monopoly: a market with a single seller offering a unique product with no close substitutes, protected from new rivals by insurmountable barriers to entry. Without entry barriers, high economic profits would quickly attract competing firms and erode the monopoly’s market power.
Barriers to entry arise from four primary sources:

Exclusive control of a key resource: A single firm owns or controls an essential input needed for production.
Government-created legal monopolies: Patents, copyrights, and exclusive public franchises legally restrict competitors from copying a product or serving a territory.
Network effects: A platform or service becomes more valuable to each user as more people join, making it difficult for smaller entrants to draw users away.
Natural monopoly (economies of scale): Massive fixed infrastructure costs cause Long-Run Average Total Cost (\(LRATC\)) to decline continuously across the entire relevant range of market demand, so one large firm can supply the entire market at lower average cost than two or more smaller competitors.

Because a single-price monopolist is the entire industry, it faces the downward-sloping market demand curve rather than a horizontal price line. Unlike a competitive price taker, a monopolist cannot sell extra units at a fixed market price. To sell one additional unit, it must lower its price—and under single pricing, that lower price applies to all units sold. Every additional sale therefore triggers two opposing effects on Total Revenue (\(TR = P \times Q\)):

Output effect (\(+P\)): Selling one more unit adds the new unit’s price to total revenue.
Price effect (\(-Q \cdot |\Delta P|\)): Lowering the price reduces revenue earned on all previous units that could have been sold at the higher price.

Because the price effect is negative for every unit beyond the first, a single-price monopolist’s Marginal Revenue (\(MR\)) always lies strictly below its demand curve (\(MR < P\)) for all positive quantities (\(Q > 0\)).






TipBring It Home: Regional Electric Grids and Pharmaceutical Patents



Two everyday industries illustrate why societies both regulate and intentionally create monopolies. A municipal water or electric distribution grid exemplifies a natural monopoly: stringing two competing sets of high-voltage power lines or water mains down every neighborhood street would waste billions in duplicate fixed capital, so one regulated utility serves the region at lower average cost. By contrast, a biotech firm granted a 20-year U.S. utility patent on a breakthrough therapy enjoys a temporary legal monopoly. Policymakers accept higher patent-protected prices during the patent window as a deliberate trade-off to incentivize risky research and development that might never occur if rivals could copy the formula immediately.




Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates why a linear inverse demand curve \(P = a - bQ\) generates a Marginal Revenue curve \(MR = a - 2bQ\) that starts at the same vertical choke price \(a\) but falls twice as steeply, crossing the horizontal axis at exactly half the choke quantity.



Figure 1. Monopoly Demand and Marginal Revenue. For linear inverse demand \(P = 100 - 2Q\), Marginal Revenue shares the vertical choke intercept (\(\$100\)) and falls twice as steeply (\(MR = 100 - 4Q\)), reaching zero at the midpoint quantity \(Q = 25\) where demand is unit elastic (\(P = \$50\)).








NoteClear It Up: Why a Monopolist Never Operates on the Inelastic Portion of Demand



Students often assume a monopolist wants demand to be inelastic so it can raise prices freely. In fact, a profit-maximizing monopolist with non-negative marginal cost (\(MC \ge 0\)) never produces in the inelastic range (\(Q > 25\) in Figure 1). In that region, \(MR < 0\): cutting output by one unit both increases total revenue and reduces total cost, strictly raising profit until the firm moves back into the elastic upper half of demand where \(MR > 0\).




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Assuming a linear inverse market demand curve \(P(Q) = a - bQ\) (with \(a > 0\) and \(b > 0\)) and single pricing across all buyers, Total Revenue is \(TR = P \cdot Q = aQ - bQ^2\), and Marginal Revenue shares the intercept \(a\) with twice the slope:
\[
MR(Q) = a - 2bQ
\]
Setting \(MR(Q) = 0\) shows that total revenue is maximized at the midpoint quantity \(Q = \frac{a}{2b}\), which is exactly half the horizontal choke quantity \(Q_{\text{choke}} = \frac{a}{b}\).






NoteWork It Out: Marginal Revenue, Output Effect, and Price Effect



Problem: A patented medical diagnostic device faces linear inverse market demand \(P = 120 - 3Q\), where \(P\) is price in dollars and \(Q\) is units sold per week.

Write the Marginal Revenue equation \(MR(Q)\).
Complete a discrete revenue schedule for \(Q = 9, 10, 11, 12\) and decompose the revenue change from \(Q = 10\) to \(Q = 11\) into its output effect and price effect.

Step-by-Step Solution:

Write the Marginal Revenue Equation: Keep the vertical intercept (\(120\)) and double the slope coefficient (\(2 \times 3 = 6\)):

\[
MR(Q) = \mathbf{120 - 6Q}
\]

Compute Price, Total Revenue, and Discrete Marginal Revenue (\(\Delta TR\)): \begin{center}

\end{center} Moving from \(Q = 10\) to \(Q = 11\) increases Total Revenue by \(\Delta TR = \$957 - \$900 = \mathbf{+\$57}\) (matching the continuous formula evaluated at the midpoint \(Q = 10.5\): \(MR(10.5) = 120 - 6(10.5) = \$57\)). This net gain equals:

Output effect: \(+\$87\) earned from selling the 11th unit.
Price effect: \(-10\text{ prior units} \times \$3\text{ discount} = -\$30\) lost on earlier units.
Net Marginal Revenue: \(\$87 - \$30 = \mathbf{+\$57}\).

Takeaway: Because selling the 11th unit requires discounting all 10 prior units by \(\$3\), discrete Marginal Revenue (\(\$57\)) sits \(\$30\) below the market price (\(\$87\)).








NoteOptional Advanced Calculus: Deriving the Output and Price Effects



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: For any differentiable inverse demand function \(P(Q)\) with \(P'(Q) < 0\), Total Revenue is \(TR(Q) = P(Q)\cdot Q\). Differentiating with respect to \(Q\) via the product rule yields:
\[
MR(Q) = \frac{d(TR)}{dQ} = \underbrace{P(Q)}_{\text{Output effect}\,(>0)} + \underbrace{Q\,\frac{dP}{dQ}}_{\text{Price effect}\,(<0)} < P(Q) \quad \text{for all } Q > 0.
\]
For the linear case \(P(Q) = a - bQ\), we have \(\frac{dP}{dQ} = -b\), so \(MR(Q) = (a - bQ) + Q(-b) = a - 2bQ\).

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
section: 8.2 Monopoly Profit Maximization and Deadweight Loss
text:
8.2 Monopoly Profit Maximization and Deadweight Loss

Conceptual Introduction
Like every profit-maximizing firm, a single-price monopolist expands output as long as the extra revenue from an additional unit exceeds its extra cost (\(MR > MC\)) and stops when the two are equal. Finding the monopoly outcome therefore follows a strict two-step rule:

Choose Quantity (\(Q_M\)): Produce the output level where Marginal Revenue equals Marginal Cost (\(MR = MC\)).
Choose Price (\(P_M\)): Move vertically up from \(Q_M\) to the demand curve to read the highest price consumers are willing to pay for that quantity.

Because \(MR < P\), setting \(MR = MC\) guarantees that the monopolist charges a price strictly above marginal cost (\(P_M > MC\)) and restricts output strictly below the socially efficient competitive quantity (\(Q_M < Q_C\), where \(P = MC\)). Those missing units between \(Q_M\) and \(Q_C\) represent mutually beneficial trades where consumers value the good more than it costs society to produce (\(MB > MC\)), yet the monopolist withholds them to keep prices elevated. The lost surplus from these unproduced units is Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)).
When a firm is a natural monopoly, breaking it into smaller competitors would push everyone up onto higher average costs. Policymakers instead rely on public regulation, facing a classic policy dilemma:

Marginal-Cost Pricing (\(P = MC\)): Restores allocative efficiency (\(DWL = \$0\)), but because \(LRATC\) is still falling, \(MC < ATC\)—so the utility suffers an economic loss and requires a taxpayer subsidy to stay open.
Average-Cost (Fair-Return) Pricing (\(P = ATC\)): Allows the utility to break even (\(\pi = \$0\)) without a subsidy while cutting prices and shrinking deadweight loss substantially compared to unregulated monopoly.







TipBring It Home: Hospital MRI Scanners and Natural Monopoly Regulation



Consider a hypothetical regional hospital operating an advanced MRI scanner with \(\$900{,}000\) in annual fixed equipment and staffing costs and a constant \(\$100\) marginal cost per scan. At \(3{,}000\) scans per year, Average Total Cost is \(\$900{,}000 / 3{,}000 + \$100 = \$400\) per scan; at \(9{,}000\) scans per year, \(ATC\) drops to \(\$900{,}000 / 9{,}000 + \$100 = \$200\) per scan. Spreading large fixed costs over higher volume continuously lowers \(ATC\)—the hallmark of natural monopoly. If the hospital faces no nearby rival and prices where \(MR = MC\), patients face a markup well above \(\$100\) and medically valuable scans go unperformed. Conversely, forcing the hospital to charge marginal cost (\(\$100\)) would leave the entire \(\$900{,}000\) fixed cost uncovered, illustrating why regulators often use fair-return pricing (\(P = ATC\)) or two-part tariffs instead.




Visual Representation
Figure 2 plots the single-price monopoly equilibrium \((Q_M, P_M)\) against the competitive benchmark \((Q_C, P_C)\) under constant marginal cost \(MC = ATC = \$20\), decomposing total potential social surplus into Consumer Surplus, Monopoly Profit, and Deadweight Loss.






NoteClear It Up: Two Classic Monopoly Misconceptions




Never read the monopoly price from the \(MR = MC\) crossing: The \(MR = MC\) intersection only determines the profit-maximizing quantity (\(Q_M\)). Once you locate \(Q_M\) on the horizontal axis, move straight up to the Demand curve to read the price (\(P_M\)) buyers actually pay.
Monopoly does not guarantee positive economic profit: Being the sole seller lets a firm choose the best point on the demand curve, not ignore costs. If market demand is weak and \(P_M < ATC\) at \(Q_M\), even a pure monopolist suffers an economic loss (and shuts down in the short run if \(P_M < AVC\)).






Figure 2. Monopoly Profit and Deadweight Loss. Equating \(MR = MC\) (open circle) sets output at \(Q_M = 20\), and reading up to demand gives \(P_M = \$60\) (\(E_M\)). Relative to the competitive benchmark \(E_C\) (\(Q_C = 40, P_C = \$20\)), the monopolist captures \(\$800\) in economic profit (teal rectangle), leaves \(\$400\) in Consumer Surplus (blue triangle), and creates \(\$400\) in Deadweight Loss (orange triangle).




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Assuming linear inverse demand \(P = a - bQ\), constant marginal cost \(MC = c\) (with \(0 \le c < a\)), and zero fixed cost (\(ATC = MC = c\)):
\[
MR = MC \implies a - 2bQ_M = c \implies Q_M = \frac{a - c}{2b}, \qquad Q_C = \frac{a - c}{b} = 2Q_M
\]
Notice that with linear demand and constant marginal cost, a single-price monopolist always cuts output to exactly half of the competitive output. The Harberger deadweight loss triangle is:
\[
DWL = \frac{1}{2}(Q_C - Q_M)(P_M - MC)
\]






NoteWork It Out: Monopoly Equilibrium, Profit, Surplus, and Deadweight Loss



Problem: Using the linear monopoly model plotted in Figure 2, suppose inverse market demand is \(P = 100 - 2Q\), Marginal Revenue is \(MR = 100 - 4Q\), and Marginal Cost is constant at \(MC = \$20\) (with zero fixed cost, so \(ATC = \$20\)). Compute \(Q_M\), \(P_M\), monopoly economic profit \(\pi_M\), monopoly Consumer Surplus \(CS_M\), the competitive benchmark \((Q_C, P_C, CS_C)\), and Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)).
Step-by-Step Solution:

Solve for Monopoly Output (\(Q_M\)) and Price (\(P_M\)): Set \(MR = MC\):

\[
100 - 4Q_M = 20 \implies 4Q_M = 80 \implies Q_M = \mathbf{20\text{ units}}
\]
Substitute \(Q_M = 20\) into the inverse demand curve:
\[
P_M = 100 - 2(20) = \mathbf{\$60}
\]

Compute Monopoly Profit (\(\pi_M\)) and Consumer Surplus (\(CS_M\)):

\[
\pi_M = (P_M - ATC) \times Q_M = (\$60 - \$20) \times 20 = \$40 \times 20 = \mathbf{\$800}
\]
\[
CS_M = \frac{1}{2} \times Q_M \times (a - P_M) = \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times (\$100 - \$60) = \mathbf{\$400}
\]

Find the Competitive Benchmark (\(Q_C, P_C, CS_C\)) and Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)): Set \(P = MC\):

\[
100 - 2Q_C = 20 \implies 2Q_C = 80 \implies Q_C = \mathbf{40\text{ units}}, \qquad P_C = \mathbf{\$20}
\]
Under constant \(MC = \$20\), competitive Producer Surplus is \(\$0\), so total competitive surplus equals Consumer Surplus:
\[
CS_C = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times (\$100 - \$20) = \mathbf{\$1{,}600}
\]
Compute the Deadweight Loss triangle:
\[
DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (40 - 20) \times (\$60 - \$20) = \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times \$40 = \mathbf{\$400}
\]
Surplus Conservation Check: \(CS_M + \pi_M + DWL = \$400 + \$800 + \$400 = \$1{,}600 = CS_C\). Compared to perfect competition, monopoly cuts output in half (from \(40\) to \(20\)), triples the price (from \(\$20\) to \(\$60\)), transfers \(\$800\) of consumer surplus into monopoly profit, and destroys \(\$400\) in deadweight loss.








NoteOptional Advanced Calculus: Profit Optimization and Welfare Integrals



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: The monopolist solves \(\max_{Q \ge 0} \pi(Q) = TR(Q) - TC(Q)\). At an interior maximum:
\[
\text{FOC: } \pi'(Q) = MR(Q) - MC(Q) = 0 \implies MR(Q_M) = MC(Q_M), \qquad \text{SOC: } \pi''(Q_M) = MR'(Q_M) - MC'(Q_M) < 0.
\]
The second-order condition requires \(MC\) to intersect \(MR\) from below. In our linear example, \(\pi''(Q) = -4 - 0 = -4 < 0\), confirming a unique global maximum. Total deadweight loss is the definite integral of net marginal social benefit over the unproduced units:
\[
DWL = \int_{Q_M}^{Q_C} \big[P(Q) - MC(Q)\big]\,dQ = \int_{20}^{40} \big[(100 - 2Q) - 20\big]\,dQ = \Big[80Q - Q^2\Big]_{20}^{40} = 1{,}600 - 1{,}200 = \$400.
\]

title: 8  Chapter 8: Monopoly, Market Power, and Price Discrimination
section: 8.3 Price Discrimination and Market Power
text:
8.3 Price Discrimination and Market Power

Conceptual Introduction
So far, we have assumed the monopolist charges every buyer the exact same price. Yet firms with market power can often earn higher profits—and sometimes expand market access—by practicing price discrimination: selling the exact same good or service to different customers at different prices not justified by cost differences. Successful price discrimination requires three conditions:

Market power: The firm must face a downward-sloping demand curve (not be a competitive price taker).
Market segmentation: The firm must be able to separate buyers according to their willingness to pay (price elasticity of demand).
Prevention of arbitrage: Buyers who receive a lower price must be unable to resell the product profitably to buyers charged a higher price.

Economists classify price discrimination into three degrees:

First-Degree (Perfect) Price Discrimination: Charging every individual buyer their exact maximum willingness to pay. Because the firm no longer has to discount prior units to make another sale, \(MR = P\). Output expands all the way to the competitive level (\(Q_C\)) and Deadweight Loss falls to zero—but the monopolist captures \(100\%\) of Total Social Surplus (\(CS = \$0\)).
Second-Degree Price Discrimination: Offering quantity discounts or tiered product menus (such as bulk warehouse packs or airline cabin classes) so customers self-select based on usage or preferences.
Third-Degree Price Discrimination: Dividing customers into observable groups (such as verified students, seniors, or business travelers) and charging a higher price to the group with less elastic (more price-insensitive) demand and a lower price to the group with more elastic (more price-sensitive) demand.







TipBring It Home: Software \texttt{.edu



Discounts and Airline Saturday-Night Stays} Software companies such as Adobe and Microsoft require verified email credentials to unlock steep academic discounts while charging full commercial rates to corporate teams. Account-level license binding prevents arbitrage (students cannot legally resell their subscription to an enterprise). Similarly, airlines separate time-sensitive business travelers (less elastic demand) from flexible leisure travelers (more elastic demand) through advance-purchase rules, non-refundable fares, and weekend-stay pricing—all while flying both passengers on the exact same aircraft.




Visual Representation
Figure 3 illustrates third-degree price discrimination for a campus theater with constant \(MC = \$4\) per ticket, equating \(MR_i = MC\) separately for the less elastic general public and more elastic student segments.



Figure 3. Third-Degree Price Discrimination. Setting \(MR_i = MC\) (open circles) independently in each separated segment yields a higher price (\(P_1^* = \$16\)) for the less elastic general public and a discounted price (\(P_2^* = \$10\)) for more price-sensitive students, generating \(\$72 + \$36 = \$108\) in combined economic profit.








NoteClear It Up: Does Price Discrimination Always Harm Consumers?



Not necessarily. First, remember that with \(MC > 0\), a profit-maximizing firm still operates on the elastic region (\(|\varepsilon_d| > 1\)) of both segments—one segment is simply less elastic than the other. Second, while price discrimination raises prices for less elastic buyers and transfers surplus to the firm, it lowers prices for more elastic buyers (such as students or seniors). Whenever discounts bring previously priced-out buyers into the market, total output expands and Deadweight Loss can fall.




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Under third-degree price discrimination with constant marginal cost \(MC\) and no resale between segments, the firm maximizes total profit by equating Marginal Revenue to Marginal Cost separately in each market:
\[
MR_1(Q_1^*) = MC, \qquad MR_2(Q_2^*) = MC
\]






NoteWork It Out: Third-Degree Price Discrimination at a Campus Theater



Problem: A campus theater faces a constant Marginal Cost of \(MC = \$4\) per ticket (with zero fixed cost) and uses photo IDs to prevent resale between two linear demand segments (plotted in Figure 3):

General Public: \(P_1 = 28 - 2Q_1 \implies MR_1 = 28 - 4Q_1\)
Students: \(P_2 = 16 - Q_2 \implies MR_2 = 16 - 2Q_2\)
Find the profit-maximizing price, quantity, and profit for each segment under third-degree price discrimination.
Compare total profit under price discrimination against charging a single uniform price to both groups.

Step-by-Step Solution:

Segmented Pricing (\(MR_i = MC\)):
General Public (\(MR_1 = 4\)):

\[
28 - 4Q_1 = 4 \implies 4Q_1 = 24 \implies Q_1^* = \mathbf{6\text{ tickets}}, \qquad P_1^* = 28 - 2(6) = \mathbf{\$16}
\]
Segment 1 profit: \(\pi_1 = (\$16 - \$4) \times 6 = \mathbf{\$72}\). * Students (\(MR_2 = 4\)):
\[
16 - 2Q_2 = 4 \implies 2Q_2 = 12 \implies Q_2^* = \mathbf{6\text{ tickets}}, \qquad P_2^* = 16 - 6 = \mathbf{\$10}
\]
Segment 2 profit: \(\pi_2 = (\$10 - \$4) \times 6 = \mathbf{\$36}\).
Combined price-discriminating output is \(Q_{\text{PD}} = 6 + 6 = \mathbf{12\text{ tickets}}\), and total profit is \(\pi_{\text{PD}} = \$72 + \$36 = \mathbf{\$108}\).

Single-Price Benchmark (\(P \le \$16\)): Solving each demand curve for quantity gives \(Q_1 = 14 - 0.5P\) and \(Q_2 = 16 - P\). Summing horizontally yields combined demand \(Q = 30 - 1.5P\), or inverse demand \(P = 20 - \frac{2}{3}Q\), with \(MR = 20 - \frac{4}{3}Q\). Setting \(MR = 4\):

\[
20 - \frac{4}{3}Q_{\text{SP}} = 4 \implies \frac{4}{3}Q_{\text{SP}} = 16 \implies Q_{\text{SP}} = \mathbf{12\text{ tickets}}, \qquad P_{\text{SP}} = 20 - \frac{2}{3}(12) = \mathbf{\$12}
\]
At \(P_{\text{SP}} = \$12\), the theater sells \(Q_1 = 8\) general-public tickets and \(Q_2 = 4\) student tickets, earning \(\pi_{\text{SP}} = (\$12 - \$4) \times 12 = \mathbf{\$96}\) (serving only the general public at \(\$16\) would earn just \(\$72\)).
Takeaway: Price discrimination raises the general-public price from \(\$12\) to \(\$16\), cuts the student price from \(\$12\) to \(\$10\), expands student attendance from \(4\) to \(6\) tickets, and increases theater profit by \(\$108 - \$96 = \mathbf{+\$12}\) (\(+12.5\%\)).








NoteOptional Advanced Calculus: The Lerner Index and Inverse-Elasticity Pricing



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Factoring \(P\) from \(MR = P + Q\frac{dP}{dQ}\) and substituting the point price elasticity of demand \(\varepsilon_d = \frac{dQ}{dP}\frac{P}{Q} < 0\) yields the Amoroso–Robinson relation:
\[
MR = P\left(1 + \frac{Q}{P}\frac{dP}{dQ}\right) = P\left(1 - \frac{1}{|\varepsilon_d|}\right).
\]
Setting \(MR = MC\) gives the Lerner Index (\(L\)) of market power:
\[
L = \frac{P - MC}{P} = \frac{1}{|\varepsilon_d|}.
\]
In perfect competition (\(|\varepsilon_d| \to \infty\)), \(L = 0\) and \(P = MC\). Under third-degree price discrimination, equating \(MR_1 = MR_2 = MC\) implies \(L_i = \frac{P_i - MC}{P_i} = \frac{1}{|\varepsilon_i|}\) in each segment. In our campus theater problem, \(|\varepsilon_1| = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{16}{6} = \frac{4}{3} \approx 1.33\) gives \(L_1 = \frac{16-4}{16} = 0.75\), while \(|\varepsilon_2| = 1\cdot\frac{10}{6} = \frac{5}{3} \approx 1.67\) gives \(L_2 = \frac{10-4}{10} = 0.60\)—confirming that both segments lie on the elastic range (\(|\varepsilon_i| > 1\)) and the less elastic segment carries the larger percentage markup.

title: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory
text:
Conceptual Introduction
Most everyday consumer markets—coffee shops, hair salons, casual restaurants, fitness studios, and clothing boutiques—do not fit neatly into either perfect competition or pure monopoly. Instead, they operate under monopolistic competition, a hybrid market structure combining three defining traits: (1) many competing sellers, (2) differentiated products (each seller offers a distinct flavor, location, brand aesthetic, or customer experience, often reinforced through non-price competition such as branding and advertising), and (3) free entry and exit in the long run.
Because its product is distinct from rivals, each monopolistically competitive firm enjoys a small degree of brand loyalty and faces a downward-sloping demand curve. Just like a monopolist, the firm maximizes short-run profit by producing where Marginal Revenue equals Marginal Cost (\(MR = MC\)) and pricing on its demand curve (\(P > MC\)). However, because there are zero barriers to entry, positive short-run economic profits attract new competitors into the neighborhood—drawing away customers and shifting each incumbent firm’s demand curve inward until economic profits are driven to zero. Conversely, short-run economic losses cause some firms to exit, shifting remaining firms’ demand outward until losses disappear.
In long-run equilibrium, the firm’s downward-sloping demand curve becomes tangent to its Average Total Cost (\(ATC\)) curve, enforcing zero economic profit (\(P = ATC\)). Yet unlike perfect competition, this tangency occurs strictly to the left of minimum \(ATC\), creating two permanent structural features: a markup over marginal cost (\(P > MC\), implying allocative inefficiency) and excess capacity (\(q_{\text{LR}} < q_{\text{eff}}\), implying productive inefficiency). Rather than pure waste, however, this tradeoff reflects the price society pays for product variety and convenience.






NoteClear It Up: Zero Economic Profit and Excess Capacity



Two common misconceptions arise in monopolistic competition:

Zero economic profit does not mean zero accounting profit. At \(P_{\text{LR}} = ATC\), the owner earns a normal profit—covering all explicit bills (rent, wages, supplies) plus the full opportunity cost of the owner’s time and invested capital.
Excess capacity is not necessarily harmful. Producing below minimum \(ATC\) raises average cost slightly, yet consumers willingly pay a small markup to enjoy diverse neighborhood options rather than one standardized product.





Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates the long-run zero-profit equilibrium of a monopolistically competitive firm, highlighting the tangency between demand and \(ATC\), the \(MR = MC\) profit-maximizing output, and the resulting excess capacity gap.



Figure 1. Long-Run Equilibrium under Monopolistic Competition. Free entry shifts demand until it is tangent to \(ATC\) at \(q_{\text{LR}}\) (where \(MR = MC\)), yielding zero economic profit (\(P_{\text{LR}} = ATC\)). Because \(q_{\text{LR}} < q_{\text{eff}}\), the firm operates with excess capacity and charges a markup above \(MC_{\text{LR}}\).




Real-World Application: Neighborhood Coffee Shops and Retail Differentiation
Walk down any busy commercial avenue and you will see independent cafés every two blocks—one roasting single-origin pour-overs, another offering oat-milk matcha and study booths, and a third specializing in quick drive-thru espresso. None earns monopoly-level economic profits for long because new cafés open whenever neighborhood rents permit, yet each operates below its physical kitchen capacity during mid-afternoon lulls so consumers can enjoy variety and convenience.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
In long-run monopolistic competition, two simultaneous conditions hold at output \(q_{\text{LR}}\):
\[
MR(q_{\text{LR}}) = MC(q_{\text{LR}}) \quad \text{(Profit Maximization)}, \qquad P(q_{\text{LR}}) = ATC(q_{\text{LR}}) \quad \text{(Zero Economic Profit)}
\]






NoteWork It Out: Long-Run Equilibrium for a Boutique Fitness Studio



Problem: Assume a boutique fitness studio in a monopolistically competitive neighborhood faces a linear long-run inverse demand curve \(P = 50 - 2q\) (where \(P\) is class price in dollars and \(q\) is daily clients) and corresponding Marginal Revenue \(MR = 50 - 4q\). Suppose the studio has fixed daily overhead of \(\$200\) and constant Marginal Cost \(MC = \$10\) per client, giving Average Total Cost \(ATC = \frac{200}{q} + 10\) (which declines over the studio’s operating range).

Find the studio’s profit-maximizing client volume \(q_{\text{LR}}\) and class price \(P_{\text{LR}}\).
Verify that the studio earns zero economic profit in the long run.
Calculate the firm’s markup over marginal cost (\(P_{\text{LR}} - MC\)).

Step-by-Step Solution:

Set \(MR = MC\) to Solve for \(q_{\text{LR}}\) and \(P_{\text{LR}}\):

\[
50 - 4q_{\text{LR}} = 10 \implies 4q_{\text{LR}} = 40 \implies q_{\text{LR}} = \mathbf{10\text{ clients per day}}
\]
Substitute \(q_{\text{LR}} = 10\) into the inverse demand curve:
\[
P_{\text{LR}} = 50 - 2(10) = \mathbf{\$30\text{ per class}}
\]

Check Long-Run Economic Profit (\(\pi\)): Compute \(ATC\) at \(q_{\text{LR}} = 10\):

\[
ATC(10) = \frac{200}{10} + 10 = 20 + 10 = \$30\text{ per class}
\]
Since \(P_{\text{LR}}\ (\$30) = ATC\ (\$30)\), economic profit is:
\[
\pi = (\$30 - \$30) \times 10 = \mathbf{\$0}
\]

Compute the Markup over Marginal Cost:

\[
\text{Markup} = P_{\text{LR}} - MC = \$30 - \$10 = \mathbf{\$20\text{ per class}}
\]
Conclusion: The studio breaks even in economic terms (\(\pi = \$0\)) while maintaining a \(\$20\) markup above marginal cost due to product differentiation.








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Proving Tangency and Excess Capacity



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Write economic profit as \(\pi(q) = q\bigl[P(q) - ATC(q)\bigr]\). In long-run equilibrium at \(q_{\text{LR}} > 0\), both zero profit (\(\pi(q_{\text{LR}}) = 0 \implies P(q_{\text{LR}}) = ATC(q_{\text{LR}})\)) and profit maximization (\(\pi'(q_{\text{LR}}) = 0\)) must hold. Applying the product rule:
\[
\pi'(q_{\text{LR}}) = \underbrace{\bigl[P(q_{\text{LR}}) - ATC(q_{\text{LR}})\bigr]}_{=\,0} + q_{\text{LR}}\bigl[P'(q_{\text{LR}}) - ATC'(q_{\text{LR}})\bigr] = 0
\]
Because \(q_{\text{LR}} > 0\), this forces \(P'(q_{\text{LR}}) = ATC'(q_{\text{LR}})\), proving that the demand curve is tangent to \(ATC\) at \(q_{\text{LR}}\). Moreover, since downward-sloping demand implies \(P'(q_{\text{LR}}) < 0\), it follows that \(ATC'(q_{\text{LR}}) < 0\): the firm must operate strictly to the left of minimum \(ATC\), mathematically guaranteeing excess capacity. (In the fitness studio problem above, \(P'(10) = -2\) and \(ATC'(10) = -200/10^2 = -2\), confirming exact tangency.)

title: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory
section: 9.2 Oligopoly, Cartels, and Strategic Interdependence
text:
9.2 Oligopoly, Cartels, and Strategic Interdependence

Conceptual Introduction
When an industry is dominated by just a handful of large firms—such as commercial aircraft manufacturing (Boeing and Airbus), wireless telecom carriers, or major airlines—the market is an oligopoly. Unlike monopolistically competitive markets with easy entry, oligopolies are protected by significant barriers to entry, including large economies of scale, control of scarce spectrum licenses, patents, or network effects. Because only a few rivals share the market, oligopolists are acutely aware of one another: every pricing decision, advertising campaign, or product launch by one firm directly affects its rivals’ sales and triggers counter-moves. Economists call this mutual awareness strategic interdependence.
Because oligopolists control the bulk of market supply, they face a powerful temptation to collude—forming a formal or informal cartel to restrict industry output and hold prices up near the monopoly level so they can split monopoly profits. However, cartels suffer from an inherent internal instability. Once a cartel sets a high price above marginal cost (\(P > MC\)), each individual member realizes it can secretly undercut the agreed price slightly, steal its rivals’ customers, and boost its own profit—until all members cheat and prices collapse back toward competitive levels.
Economists measure industry concentration using two standard tools: the Four-Firm Concentration Ratio (\(CR_4\)), which sums the market shares of the four largest firms, and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (\(HHI\)), which sums the squared market shares of all firms in the market (\(HHI = \sum_{i=1}^N s_i^2\)). Antitrust regulators at the Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission scrutinize mergers that sharply increase the \(HHI\).


Visual Representation
Figure 2 contrasts market outcomes along a quantity-price continuum under linear market demand and constant marginal cost, showing how a non-cooperative oligopoly settles strictly between the collusive cartel benchmark (\(Q_{\text{cartel}}, P_{\text{cartel}}\)) and the competitive benchmark (\(Q_C, P_C\)).



Figure 2. The Oligopoly Output-Price Spectrum. When oligopolists fail to sustain a cartel, non-cooperative competition expands industry output beyond \(Q_{\text{cartel}}\) and lowers price below \(P_{\text{cartel}}\), moving the market closer to the competitive outcome \((Q_C, P_C)\).




Real-World Application: OPEC Production Quotas and Cheating Incentives
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) acts as an international oil cartel, agreeing on production quotas to keep global crude oil prices elevated. As an illustrative example, if OPEC restricts output and pushes crude oil to \(\$90\) per barrel while a member country’s marginal extraction cost is only \(\$20\) per barrel, that member faces an immediate temptation to quietly pump above its assigned quota—earning an extra \(\$70\) per barrel—until rival members detect the cheating and quotas break down.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (\(HHI\)) squares each firm’s percentage market share \(s_i\) (expressed as a number from \(0\) to \(100\)):
\[
HHI = s_1^2 + s_2^2 + \dots + s_N^2
\]
A pure monopoly (\(s_1 = 100\)) has the maximum \(HHI = 100^2 = 10{,}000\), whereas an industry split among many tiny firms approaches \(HHI \approx 0\).






NoteWork It Out: Measuring Concentration and Evaluating a Horizontal Merger



Problem: Suppose a regional wireless internet market is served by four providers with market shares of \(40\%\), \(30\%\), \(20\%\), and \(10\%\).

Compute the Four-Firm Concentration Ratio (\(CR_4\)) and the baseline \(HHI\).
Compute the new post-merger \(HHI\) and the change in \(HHI\) (\(\Delta HHI\)) if the two smallest providers (\(20\%\) and \(10\%\)) merge into a single \(30\%\) firm (assuming customer shares initially combine without defection).

Step-by-Step Solution:

Calculate Baseline \(CR_4\) and \(HHI\):

\[
CR_4 = 40\% + 30\% + 20\% + 10\% = \mathbf{100\%}
\]
\[
HHI_{\text{pre}} = 40^2 + 30^2 + 20^2 + 10^2 = 1{,}600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = \mathbf{3{,}000}
\]

Calculate Post-Merger \(HHI\) (Shares: \(40\%\), \(30\%\), \(30\%\)) and \(\Delta HHI\):

\[
HHI_{\text{post}} = 40^2 + 30^2 + 30^2 = 1{,}600 + 900 + 900 = \mathbf{3{,}400}
\]
\[
\Delta HHI = HHI_{\text{post}} - HHI_{\text{pre}} = 3{,}400 - 3{,}000 = \mathbf{+400\text{ points}}
\]
Algebraic check: When two firms with shares \(s_A\) and \(s_B\) merge, \((s_A + s_B)^2 - (s_A^2 + s_B^2) = 2 s_A s_B = 2(20)(10) = 400\).
Conclusion: Notice that \(CR_4\) stays unchanged at \(100\%\), yet the \(HHI\) rises by \(400\) points (from \(3{,}000\) to \(3{,}400\)), highlighting why antitrust regulators rely on \(HHI\) to flag highly concentrated oligopoly mergers for review.

title: 9  Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory
section: 9.3 Game Theory, Dominant Strategies, and Nash Equilibrium
text:
9.3 Game Theory, Dominant Strategies, and Nash Equilibrium

Conceptual Introduction
Because oligopolists cannot make decisions in a vacuum, economists analyze their behavior using game theory—the mathematical study of strategic decision-making when each player’s payoff depends on the actions of other players. Every strategic game consists of three building blocks: (1) the players, (2) the strategies available to each player, and (3) the payoffs resulting from every combination of choices.
To predict how rational rivals will behave without binding contracts, economists look for two key concepts:

Dominant Strategy: A strategy that yields a strictly higher payoff for a player no matter what strategy the rival chooses. If a player has a dominant strategy, they will always play it.
Nash Equilibrium: An outcome in which every player is choosing their best response given what the other players are doing. At a Nash equilibrium, no player can improve their own payoff by unilaterally changing their strategy.

The most famous game in economics is the Prisoner’s Dilemma. In this game, both firms could earn higher joint profits by cooperating (e.g., keeping prices high or limiting advertising), yet each firm’s individual dominant strategy is to defect (slash prices or flood the market with ads). As a result, rational self-interest locks both firms into a non-cooperative Nash equilibrium where both earn lower profits!


Visual Representation
Figure 3 presents a \(2 \times 2\) payoff matrix for two competing streaming platforms deciding simultaneously between keeping subscription prices high (\(\$18\)) or discounting to capture subscribers (\(\$12\)).






NoteClear It Up: Why Prisoners’ Dilemmas Are Good News for Consumers



In a business pricing game, failure to cooperate traps rival firms in a low-price Nash equilibrium—which hurts the firms’ combined profits, yet benefits consumers through lower prices and higher consumer surplus! Antitrust laws exist specifically to prevent oligopolists from escaping their Prisoner’s Dilemma through illegal price-fixing agreements.





Figure 3. A \(2 \times 2\) Pricing Prisoner’s Dilemma (Annual Profits in Millions). Underlined payoffs show each firm’s best response. Both firms have a dominant strategy to Discount (\(\$12\)), landing in the bottom-right Nash equilibrium (\(\$35\text{M}, \$35\text{M}\)) rather than the cooperative outcome (\(\$50\text{M}, \$50\text{M}\)).




Real-World Application: Airline Fare Wars and Repeated Interaction
When two airlines compete on the same nonstop route (such as San Francisco to Los Angeles), matching a competitor’s fare cut within hours via automated pricing software acts as a tit-for-tat enforcement mechanism. Because airlines interact repeatedly day after day rather than playing a one-shot game, the credible threat of immediate retaliation helps stabilize fares without explicit collusion.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
To solve any \(2 \times 2\) simultaneous game for a Nash equilibrium, evaluate each player’s conditional best responses:
\[
\text{Strategy } s_A^* \text{ is a Best Response to } s_B^* \iff \pi_A(s_A^*, s_B^*) \ge \pi_A(s_A, s_B^*) \quad \forall s_A
\]






NoteWork It Out: Solving a Simultaneous Pricing Game



Problem: Using the simultaneous one-shot payoff matrix in Figure 3, prove mathematically why Discount (\(\$12\)) is a strictly dominant strategy for Firm A and verify that (Discount, Discount) is the unique Nash equilibrium.
Step-by-Step Solution:

Check Firm A’s Best Response When Firm B Plays ``Price High (\(\$18\))’’: Compare Firm A’s profit in the left column:

\[
\pi_A(\text{Discount} \mid \text{B High}) = \$65\text{M} > \pi_A(\text{High} \mid \text{B High}) = \$50\text{M}
\]
Firm A earns \(\$15\text{M}\) more by discounting.

Check Firm A’s Best Response When Firm B Plays ``Discount (\(\$12\))’’: Compare Firm A’s profit in the right column:

\[
\pi_A(\text{Discount} \mid \text{B Discount}) = \$35\text{M} > \pi_A(\text{High} \mid \text{B Discount}) = \$20\text{M}
\]
Firm A again earns \(\$15\text{M}\) more by discounting.

Confirm Dominant Strategy and Nash Equilibrium: Because Discount yields a strictly higher payoff regardless of Firm B’s choice, Discount is Firm A’s strictly dominant strategy. By symmetry, Discount is also Firm B’s strictly dominant strategy. At (Discount, Discount), neither firm can raise its profit above \(\$35\text{M}\) by switching unilaterally to High (which drops its profit to \(\$20\text{M}\)).

Conclusion: (Discount, Discount) with payoffs \((\$35\text{M}, \$35\text{M})\) is the unique Nash equilibrium, even though both firms would earn \(\$50\text{M}\) each if they could credibly cooperate.








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Cournot Duopoly Best-Response Functions



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: In a continuous quantity-setting Cournot duopoly facing linear market inverse demand \(P = 100 - (q_1 + q_2)\) with symmetric constant marginal cost \(MC = 10\), Firm 1 chooses \(q_1\) to maximize \(\pi_1 = [100 - q_1 - q_2]q_1 - 10q_1 = 90q_1 - q_1^2 - q_1 q_2\). Setting \(\frac{\partial \pi_1}{\partial q_1} = 90 - 2q_1 - q_2 = 0\) yields Firm 1’s continuous best-response function:
\[
q_1^*(q_2) = 45 - \frac{1}{2}q_2
\]
By symmetry, \(q_2^*(q_1) = 45 - \frac{1}{2}q_1\). Solving simultaneously gives the Cournot-Nash equilibrium output \(q_1^* = q_2^* = 30\) (total output \(Q = 60\), price \(P = \$40\), profit \(\pi_i = \$900\) each), lying strictly between the cartel output (\(Q_M = 45, P_M = \$55\)) and competitive output (\(Q_C = 90, P_C = \$10\)).

title: 10  Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources
text:
Conceptual Introduction
In Chapter 4, we showed that competitive markets maximize total social surplus when private buyers and sellers capture all benefits and pay all costs of a transaction (\(MB = MC\)). However, markets fail to allocate resources efficiently whenever production or consumption creates an externality—an uncompensated cost or benefit imposed on a third party outside the market transaction.
Externalities split into two fundamental categories:

Negative Externalities (External Costs): When producing or consuming a good imposes unpriced harm on bystanders—such as industrial air pollution, highway traffic congestion, or late-night noise—the Marginal Social Cost (\(MSC\)) exceeds the firm’s Marginal Private Cost (\(MPC\)) by the Marginal External Cost (\(MEC\)): \(MSC = MPC + MEC\). Because unregulated firms ignore \(MEC\) and produce where \(MB = MPC\), the free market overproduces (\(Q_M > Q^*\)), creating a Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)) triangle on the excess units whose social cost exceeds social benefit.
Positive Externalities (External Benefits): When an activity generates unpriced spillover benefits for third parties—such as vaccinations reducing disease transmission, basic scientific research, or neighborhood historic preservation—the Marginal Social Benefit (\(MSB\)) exceeds Marginal Private Benefit (\(MPB\)) by the Marginal External Benefit (\(MEB\)): \(MSB = MPB + MEB\). Left alone, the market produces where \(MPB = MC\) and underproduces (\(Q_M < Q^*\)), forfeiting mutually beneficial surplus on the missing units.







NoteClear It Up: Why the Socially Optimal Level of Pollution Is Rarely Zero



Students often assume that because pollution causes real harm, the economically efficient level of emissions must be zero. In reality, eliminating the very last unit of emissions from electricity generation, shipping, or manufacturing often requires shutting down vital economic activity whose marginal benefit vastly exceeds the marginal damage of a small amount of pollution (\(MB > MSC\)). Social efficiency balances incremental benefits against incremental social costs at \(MB = MSC\) (\(Q^* > 0\)), curbing only those units where marginal social harm exceeds marginal benefit.




Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates a negative production externality under three simplifying assumptions: a competitive market, linear marginal benefit and marginal private cost schedules, and a constant marginal external cost (\(MEC = \$10\) per unit). Because \(MSC\) lies vertically above \(MPC\) by \(MEC\), unregulated market output \(Q_M = 40\) exceeds the socially efficient output \(Q^* = 35\), generating the shaded Deadweight Loss triangle on the five overproduced units.



Figure 1. Negative Production Externality. Because firms ignore Marginal External Cost (\(MEC = \$10\)), the unregulated market reaches \(E_M\) at \(Q_M = 40\) (\(MB = MPC\)) instead of the socially optimal \(E^*\) at \(Q^* = 35\) (\(MB = MSC\)). On units \(35\) through \(40\), \(MSC\) exceeds \(MB\), generating a Deadweight Loss of \(\$25\).








TipBring It Home: Urban Traffic Congestion and Carbon Emissions



Every weekday morning on congested metropolitan highways and bridges, each additional commuter who merges onto the roadway considers only their private travel time and fuel expense (\(MPC\)). Yet their car slows down thousands of drivers behind them, imposing an unpriced congestion externality (\(MEC\)) in lost time and extra idling emissions. Dynamic tolling—such as peak-hour bridge tolls or express-lane congestion pricing—attempts to price that external delay so drivers weigh the full social cost of rush-hour travel.
A similar gap separates private decisions from social costs in energy markets. Industrial and transportation fossil-fuel combustion releases greenhouse gases whose climate damages fall globally outside the private transaction. Empirical analysis carefully distinguishes physical emissions volumes—such as annual U.S. energy-related carbon dioxide emissions compiled by the U.S. Energy Information Administration and published on St. Louis Fed FRED under series (measured in million metric tons of \(\text{CO}_2\))—from the estimated dollar marginal external damage per ton (the social cost of carbon).




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Comparing unregulated equilibrium (\(MB = MPC\)) with social efficiency (\(MB = MSC = MPC + MEC\)) under linear curves and a constant marginal external cost yields a triangular deadweight loss whose base is the overproduced quantity \((Q_M - Q^*)\) and whose height is \(MEC(Q_M) = MSC(Q_M) - MB(Q_M)\):
\[
MSC(Q) = MPC(Q) + MEC(Q), \qquad DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (Q_M - Q^*) \times MEC(Q_M)
\]






NoteWork It Out: Quantifying Overproduction and Deadweight Loss



Problem: Using the linear competitive market in Figure 1, suppose marginal benefit is \(MB = 100 - Q\), marginal private cost is \(MPC = 20 + Q\), and marginal external cost is constant at \(MEC = \$10\) per unit (assuming no consumption externalities, so \(MSB = MB\)). Compute the unregulated outcome \((Q_M, P_M)\), the socially efficient outcome \((Q^*, P^*)\), and the Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)) from unregulated production.
Step-by-Step Solution:

Find Unregulated Equilibrium (\(Q_M, P_M\)) Where \(MB = MPC\):

\[
100 - Q_M = 20 + Q_M \implies 2Q_M = 80 \implies Q_M = \mathbf{40\text{ units}}
\]
Substitute \(Q_M = 40\) into \(MB\):
\[
P_M = 100 - 40 = \mathbf{\$60}
\]

Construct \(MSC\) and Find Efficient Equilibrium (\(Q^*, P^*\)) Where \(MB = MSC\):

\[
MSC = MPC + MEC = (20 + Q) + 10 = 30 + Q
\]
Set \(MB = MSC\):
\[
100 - Q^* = 30 + Q^* \implies 2Q^* = 70 \implies Q^* = \mathbf{35\text{ units}}, \qquad P^* = 100 - 35 = \mathbf{\$65}
\]

Compute Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)) from the Five Overproduced Units: At \(Q_M = 40\), \(MSC(40) = 30 + 40 = \$70\) while \(MB(40) = \$60\), confirming the vertical gap \(MSC(40) - MB(40) = \$10 = MEC\):

\[
DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (Q_M - Q^*) \times MEC = \frac{1}{2} \times (40 - 35) \times \$10 = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times \$10 = \mathbf{\$25}
\]
Conclusion: Ignoring the \(\$10\) per-unit external damage causes the market to overproduce by \(5\) units at an artificially low price (\(\$60\) vs. \(\$65\)), destroying \(\$25\) in net social welfare.








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Calculus of Social Surplus and Deadweight Loss



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Let \(TB(Q)\) be Total Benefit, \(TPC(Q)\) be Total Private Cost, and \(TEC(Q)\) be Total External Cost. Maximizing Net Social Benefit \(NSB(Q) = TB(Q) - TPC(Q) - TEC(Q)\) requires the first-order condition:
\[
\frac{d(NSB)}{dQ} = MB(Q^*) - MPC(Q^*) - MEC(Q^*) = 0 \implies MB(Q^*) = MSC(Q^*)
\]
For any overproduced market quantity \(Q_M > Q^*\), exact Deadweight Loss equals the definite integral of excess marginal social cost over marginal benefit:
\[
DWL = \int_{Q^*}^{Q_M} \bigl[MSC(Q) - MB(Q)\bigr]\,dQ
\]
In Figure 1, \(MSC(Q) - MB(Q) = (30 + Q) - (100 - Q) = 2Q - 70\), so:
\[
DWL = \int_{35}^{40} (2Q - 70)\,dQ = \bigl[Q^2 - 70Q\bigr]_{35}^{40} = (1{,}600 - 2{,}800) - (1{,}225 - 2{,}450) = -1{,}200 - (-1{,}225) = \$25
\]
