title: 13  Chapter 13: Asymmetric Information, Risk, and Market Design
section: 13.3 Expected Value, Risk Aversion, and Expected Utility
text:
13.3 Expected Value, Risk Aversion, and Expected Utility

Conceptual Introduction
Why are households willing to pay insurance premiums that exceed their average annual claim payouts? Because most people exhibit diminishing marginal utility of wealth: gaining an extra \(\$1{,}000\) when you are already comfortable adds less happiness than losing \(\$1{,}000\) hurts when you are struggling to pay rent. Consequently, most individuals are risk averse—given two prospects with the exact same average dollar payoff, a risk-averse person strictly prefers a guaranteed certain outcome over a risky gamble. (By contrast, a risk-neutral agent cares only about average dollar payoffs, and a risk-loving agent prefers the gamble over its guaranteed expected value.)
To model decisions under uncertainty, economists distinguish four closely linked concepts:

Expected Value (\(E[W]\)): The probability-weighted average of dollar outcomes across all possible states of the world.
Expected Utility (\(EU\)): The probability-weighted average of the utility generated by wealth in each state. A risk-averse agent has a strictly concave utility function \(u(W)\) and maximizes Expected Utility.
Certainty Equivalent (\(CE\)): The guaranteed dollar wealth that yields the exact same utility as the risky prospect (\(u(CE) = EU\)). For a risk-averse person, \(CE < E[W]\).
Risk Premium (\(RP\)): The gap \(E[W] - CE\), representing the maximum extra dollar amount above the actuarially fair expected loss that a risk-averse person is willing to pay to eliminate risk completely. An actuarially fair insurance policy sets its premium exactly equal to expected loss.







NoteClear It Up: Why Insurance Companies Can Profit While Customers Benefit



An insurance company pools thousands of largely independent risks across many households, using the Law of Large Numbers to diversify away randomness so its average payout per customer is highly predictable. Because risk-averse households gain utility by trading an uncertain catastrophic loss for a predictable annual premium, insurance creates mutual gains from trade even when premiums include an administrative markup above the actuarially fair expected loss—provided that markup does not exceed the customer’s risk premium.




Visual Representation
Figure 3 plots a concave utility-of-wealth curve \(u(W)\) for a risk-averse individual facing a \(50/50\) gamble between low wealth \(W_1\) and high wealth \(W_2\). Because \(u(W)\) bends downward (diminishing marginal utility), the straight chord connecting \((W_1, u(W_1))\) and \((W_2, u(W_2))\) lies strictly below the curve. At the midpoint \(E[W]\), the gamble’s expected utility \(EU\) falls below the utility of receiving \(E[W]\) with certainty, \(u(E[W])\). Reading horizontally across from \(EU\) back to the utility curve identifies the certainty equivalent \(CE < E[W]\); the horizontal gap \(E[W] - CE\) is the individual’s risk premium.



Figure 3. Concave Utility and Risk Aversion. Because \(u(W)\) bends downward (diminishing marginal utility of wealth), the expected utility of a \(50/50\) gamble (\(EU\)) lies below the utility of certain expected wealth \(u(E[W])\). The horizontal distance \(E[W] - CE\) is the risk premium.








TipBring It Home: Why You Should Insure Your Home—Not Your Toaster



Expected utility theory offers a practical rule for personal finance: insure against catastrophic wealth shocks, and self-insure small, affordable losses.

Catastrophic Losses (Large Curvature, Large Risk Premium): A house fire, major liability lawsuit, or extended hospitalization can wipe out a huge fraction of a household’s lifetime wealth. Across such a wide wealth swing, the utility curve \(u(W)\) bends sharply downward, making the household’s risk premium very large relative to expected loss—so paying an insurer’s markup is well worth it.
Small Losses (Nearly Linear Segment, Tiny Risk Premium): Over a narrow \(\$150\) swing—such as a cracked smartphone screen or a broken small kitchen appliance—the concave utility curve \(u(W)\) is nearly a straight line. Because the household is almost risk neutral over tiny losses, its risk premium is pennies, whereas retail extended warranties typically carry steep administrative markups.





Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
For two wealth states \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) occurring with probabilities \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) (\(p_1 + p_2 = 1\)), Expected Wealth and Expected Utility are:
\[
E[W] = p_1 W_1 + p_2 W_2, \qquad EU = p_1 u(W_1) + p_2 u(W_2)
\]
The Certainty Equivalent \(CE\) solves \(u(CE) = EU\), the Risk Premium is \(RP = E[W] - CE\), and a household with initial wealth \(W_0\) facing a potential loss is willing to pay a maximum full-insurance premium of:
\[
\text{Max Premium} = W_0 - CE = \text{Expected Loss} + RP
\]






NoteWork It Out: Expected Utility, Certainty Equivalent, and Maximum Premium



Problem: A graduate student has initial wealth \(W_0 = \$10{,}000\) and utility of wealth \(u(W) = \sqrt{W}\). During the academic year, there is a \(20\%\) probability (\(p = 0.20\)) that their laptop and equipment are stolen, causing a \(\$6{,}400\) loss (leaving \(W_1 = \$3{,}600\)), and an \(80\%\) probability (\(1 - p = 0.80\)) of no loss (\(W_2 = \$10{,}000\)).

Calculate the Expected Loss and Expected Wealth \(E[W]\) without insurance.
Calculate Expected Utility \(EU\) without insurance, and find the Certainty Equivalent wealth \(CE\) (where \(\sqrt{CE} = EU\)).
Determine the student’s Risk Premium and the maximum insurance premium they would be willing to pay for full coverage.

Step-by-Step Solution:

Compute Expected Loss and Expected Wealth (\(E[W]\)):

\[
\text{Expected Loss} = 0.20 \times \$6{,}400 = \mathbf{\$1{,}280}
\]
\[
E[W] = 0.20(\$3{,}600) + 0.80(\$10{,}000) = \$720 + \$8{,}000 = \mathbf{\$8{,}720}
\]

Compute Expected Utility (\(EU\)) and Certainty Equivalent (\(CE\)):

\[
EU = 0.20\sqrt{3{,}600} + 0.80\sqrt{10{,}000} = 0.20(60) + 0.80(100) = 12 + 80 = \mathbf{92\text{ utils}}
\]
Solve \(\sqrt{CE} = 92\) for the Certainty Equivalent:
\[
CE = 92^2 = \mathbf{\$8{,}464}
\]

Calculate Risk Premium and Maximum Willingness to Pay:

\[
\text{Risk Premium} = E[W] - CE = \$8{,}720 - \$8{,}464 = \mathbf{\$256}
\]
\[
\text{Max Premium} = W_0 - CE = \$10{,}000 - \$8{,}464 = \mathbf{\$1{,}536}
\]
Notice that \(\$1{,}536\) decomposes cleanly into the \(\$1{,}280\) actuarially fair expected loss plus the \(\$256\) risk premium (\(\$1{,}280 + \$256 = \$1{,}536\)).
Conclusion: Because the student is risk averse, they gain utility by purchasing full coverage at any premium up to \(\$1{,}536\)—allowing an insurer to earn up to \(\$256\) in loading/markup above expected claims while still leaving the student better off.








NoteOptional Advanced Section: Arrow-Pratt Measure of Risk Aversion



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: For a twice-differentiable utility function \(u(W)\) with positive marginal utility (\(u'(W) > 0\)), risk aversion requires strict concavity (\(u''(W) < 0\)). Economists measure the curvature of utility using the Arrow-Pratt Coefficient of Absolute Risk Aversion:
\[
A(W) = -\frac{u''(W)}{u'(W)} > 0
\]
For \(u(W) = \sqrt{W} = W^{1/2}\), differentiating yields \(u'(W) = \frac{1}{2}W^{-1/2}\) and \(u''(W) = -\frac{1}{4}W^{-3/2}\), giving:
\[
A(W) = -\frac{-\frac{1}{4}W^{-3/2}}{\frac{1}{2}W^{-1/2}} = \frac{1}{2W}
\]
Because \(A'(W) = -\frac{1}{2W^2} < 0\), this utility function exhibits decreasing absolute risk aversion: a wealthier household is willing to accept a fixed-dollar gamble more readily than a poorer household. Its corresponding Coefficient of Relative Risk Aversion, \(R(W) = W \cdot A(W) = \frac{1}{2}\), is constant across all wealth levels.

title: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism
text:
1. Conceptual Introduction
In Chapter 2, we saw that specialization according to comparative advantage expands consumption beyond domestic production limits. Now we use supply, demand, and surplus analysis to pinpoint who wins and who loses inside a country when it opens its borders to international trade.
To determine whether a small open economy becomes an importer or an exporter of a specific good, compare its autarky (no-trade) domestic equilibrium price (\(P_d\)) against the prevailing world price (\(P_w\)):

Importing Country (\(P_w < P_d\)): Foreign producers have a comparative advantage and can supply the good cheaper than domestic firms. Under free trade, the domestic price drops to \(P_w\). Domestic consumers cheer—buying more at a lower price and capturing a massive expansion in Consumer Surplus (\(CS\)). Domestic producers hurt—cutting production and losing Producer Surplus (\(PS\)). However, the gain to consumers strictly exceeds the loss to domestic producers, creating a net gain in Total Social Surplus.
Exporting Country (\(P_w > P_d\)): Domestic producers have a comparative advantage and can sell abroad at a higher world price. Under free trade, the domestic price rises to \(P_w\). Domestic producers expand output and gain more Producer Surplus than domestic consumers lose in Consumer Surplus—once again increasing net Total Social Surplus.

This sharp distributional split explains why trade policy is always politically contentious: the gains from free trade are spread thinly across millions of consumers (e.g., saving \(\$30\) on a pair of shoes), whereas the losses are concentrated among specific domestic factories and workers who lobby intensely for protection.


2. Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates an importing market where the world price \(P_w\) lies below the autarky price \(P_d\), expanding total social surplus by the green shaded triangle.



Figure 1. Welfare Gains from Free Trade (Importing Case). When \(P_w = \$40 < P_d = \$60\), domestic production falls to \(10\) and domestic consumption rises to \(30\), generating \(20\) units of imports and a net gain in Total Social Surplus (green triangle).




3. Real-World Application: Global Apparel and Consumer Electronics Trade
When U.S. retailers import smartphones, laptops, and apparel from specialized global supply chains at lower world prices, American households save thousands of dollars per year on everyday goods—expanding Consumer Surplus across the entire economy, even as domestic apparel manufacturing employment contracts.


4. Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
At world price \(P_w < P_d\), import volume and net social surplus gain are:
\[
\text{Imports} = Q_d(P_w) - Q_s(P_w), \qquad \Delta TS_{\text{trade}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Imports} \times (P_d - P_w)
\]
Worked Problem: In a small country’s market for steel, domestic inverse demand is \(P_d = 100 - 2Q\) and domestic inverse supply is \(P_s = 20 + 2Q\).

Find the autarky equilibrium price \(P_d^*\) and quantity \(Q_d^*\).
Suppose the country opens to free trade at a world price of \(P_w = \$40\) per ton. Calculate domestic quantity supplied, domestic quantity demanded, import volume, and the net gain in Total Social Surplus (\(\Delta TS\)).

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Find Autarky Equilibrium (\(P_d^*, Q_d^*\)): Set demand equal to supply:

\[
100 - 2Q = 20 + 2Q \implies 80 = 4Q \implies Q_d^* = \mathbf{20\text{ tons}}, \qquad P_d^* = 100 - 2(20) = \mathbf{\$60}
\]

Find Quantities and Imports at \(P_w = \$40\):

\[
40 = 20 + 2Q_s \implies 2Q_s = 20 \implies Q_s = \mathbf{10\text{ tons produced domestically}}
\]
\[
40 = 100 - 2Q_d \implies 2Q_d = 60 \implies Q_d = \mathbf{30\text{ tons consumed domestically}}
\]
\[
\text{Imports} = Q_d - Q_s = 30 - 10 = \mathbf{20\text{ tons}}
\]

Calculate Net Social Surplus Gain (\(\Delta TS\)):

\[
\Delta TS = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Imports} \times (P_d^* - P_w) = \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times (\$60 - \$40) = 10 \times \$20 = \mathbf{+\$200}
\]
Conclusion: Opening to free trade generates \(20\) tons of steel imports and increases national social welfare by \(+\$200\).
crumbs: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism

title: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism
section: 14.2 Tariffs, Import Quotas, and Deadweight Loss
text:
14.2 Tariffs, Import Quotas, and Deadweight Loss

Conceptual Introduction
To shield domestic industries from foreign competition, governments frequently impose trade barriers—most commonly a tariff (a per-unit or percentage tax levied on imported goods) or an import quota (a legal cap on the physical quantity of a good allowed to enter the country). In our small open economy benchmark, foreign supply at the world price \(P_w\) is perfectly elastic, so imposing a per-unit tariff \(t\) raises the domestic market price by the full amount of the tariff, from \(P_w\) to \(P_t = P_w + t\).
This price increase triggers four distinct welfare effects relative to free trade, traditionally labeled Areas \(A, B, C,\) and \(D\):

Consumer Surplus Shrinks by \(-(A + B + C + D)\): Domestic buyers pay a higher price (\(P_w + t\)) and cut consumption from \(Q_{d1}\) to \(Q_{d2}\).
Producer Surplus Expands by \(+A\): Protected by the higher domestic price, domestic producers expand output from \(Q_{s1}\) to \(Q_{s2}\). Area \(A\) is a direct transfer from domestic consumers to domestic firms.
Government Tariff Revenue Equals \(+C = t \times (Q_{d2} - Q_{s2})\): The domestic treasury collects \(t\) dollars on every imported unit that still crosses the border.
Deadweight Loss Equals \(-(B + D)\): Area \(B\) represents production inefficiency (using higher-cost domestic resources to produce units that could have been imported cheaply at \(P_w\)), while Area \(D\) represents consumption inefficiency (mutually beneficial trades lost when buyers whose willingness to pay exceeds \(P_w\) are priced out at \(P_w + t\)).

An import quota restricting imports to the exact same volume (\(Q_{d2} - Q_{s2}\)) pushes the domestic price to the same level \(P_w + t\) and causes the exact same deadweight loss \((B + D)\)—with one critical difference. Instead of generating domestic tax revenue, Area \(C\) becomes quota rents captured by whoever holds the valuable import licenses. If licenses are given away to foreign exporters (as under a voluntary export restraint), Area \(C\) flows abroad, increasing the importing country’s net welfare loss from \(B + D\) to \(B + C + D\). In practice, when tariffs or quotas raise the domestic price of intermediate inputs such as steel or solar panels, domestic producers capture Area \(A\), while downstream manufacturers—such as automakers, construction firms, and rooftop solar installers—face higher input costs that squeeze margins and raise retail prices.






NoteClear It Up: Why Tariffs Create Two Deadweight Loss Triangles (\(B + D\))



Unlike a domestic excise tax (which creates a single Harberger deadweight loss triangle), an import tariff creates two separate deadweight loss triangles. Triangle \(B\) wastes productive resources by pulling higher-cost domestic suppliers into production above \(P_w\), while Triangle \(D\) destroys consumer surplus by pricing out domestic buyers who value the good above \(P_w\) but below \(P_w + t\).




Visual Representation
Figure 2 illustrates the four welfare regions (\(A, B, C, D\)) created when a per-unit tariff of \(t = \$10\) raises the domestic steel price from \(P_w = \$40\) to \(P_w + t = \$50\). Table~\(\ref{tab:tariff_vs_quota}\) compares the welfare incidence of a tariff against an equivalent import quota.



Figure 2. Welfare Effects of an Import Tariff. A \(\$10\) per-unit tariff raises domestic price from \(\$40\) to \(\$50\), cutting imports from \(20\) to \(10\) tons. Consumers lose \(A+B+C+D\), domestic producers gain \(A\), the government collects tariff revenue \(C\), and society suffers deadweight loss \(B+D\).




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra-First)
Under a per-unit tariff \(t\) raising the domestic price from \(P_w\) to \(P_t = P_w + t\):
\[
\text{Area } A = \frac{Q_{s1} + Q_{s2}}{2} \times t, \qquad \text{Tariff Revenue } (C) = t \times (Q_{d2} - Q_{s2})
\]
\[
DWL = B + D = \frac{1}{2} t (Q_{s2} - Q_{s1}) + \frac{1}{2} t (Q_{d1} - Q_{d2}), \qquad \Delta CS = -(A + B + C + D)
\]






NoteWork It Out 14.2: Welfare Impact of a $10 Steel Tariff vs. a 10-Ton Quota



Continuing our steel market (\(P = 100 - 2Q_d\), \(P = 20 + 2Q_s\), \(P_w = \$40\)), suppose the government imposes a per-unit tariff of \(t = \$10\) per ton, raising the domestic price to \(P_t = \$50\).

Compute post-tariff domestic supply (\(Q_{s2}\)), domestic demand (\(Q_{d2}\)), and post-tariff imports.
Calculate Areas \(A, B, C,\) and \(D\), total Consumer Surplus loss (\(\Delta CS\)), and net Deadweight Loss (\(DWL\)).
How does net domestic welfare change if the government replaces the tariff with a \(10\)-ton import quota and allocates import licenses free of charge to foreign exporters?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Post-Tariff Quantities at \(P_t = \$50\):

\[
50 = 20 + 2Q_{s2} \implies 2Q_{s2} = 30 \implies Q_{s2} = \mathbf{15\text{ tons}}
\]
\[
50 = 100 - 2Q_{d2} \implies 2Q_{d2} = 50 \implies Q_{d2} = \mathbf{25\text{ tons}}
\]
Post-tariff imports fall from \(20\) tons down to \(25 - 15 = \mathbf{10\text{ tons}}\).

Compute Areas \(A, B, C, D\) and Verify \(\Delta CS\):
Producer Surplus Gain (Trapezoid \(A\)):

\[
\text{Area } A = \frac{Q_{s1} + Q_{s2}}{2} \times t = \frac{10 + 15}{2} \times \$10 = 12.5 \times \$10 = \mathbf{\$125}
\]

Government Tariff Revenue (Rectangle \(C\)):

\[
\text{Area } C = t \times \text{Imports}_{\text{tariff}} = \$10 \times 10 = \mathbf{\$100}
\]

Deadweight Loss Triangles (\(B\) and \(D\)):

\[
\text{Area } B = \frac{1}{2}(15 - 10)(\$10) = \mathbf{\$25}, \qquad \text{Area } D = \frac{1}{2}(30 - 25)(\$10) = \mathbf{\$25}
\]
\[
DWL = B + D = \$25 + \$25 = \mathbf{\$50}
\]

Cross-Check Consumer Surplus Loss: Summing all four areas gives \(\Delta CS = -(\$125 + \$25 + \$100 + \$25) = \mathbf{-\$275}\). Checking directly against the free-trade consumer surplus (\(CS_{\text{trade}} = \$900\)):

\[
CS_{\text{tariff}} = \frac{1}{2}(25)(\$100 - \$50) = \$625 \implies \Delta CS = \$625 - \$900 = \mathbf{-\$275} \quad \checkmark
\]

Equivalent 10-Ton Quota with Foreign License Holders: Capping imports at \(10\) tons holds the domestic price at \(\$50\) and generates the same \(\Delta CS = -\$275\) and \(\Delta PS = +\$125\). However, Area \(C = \$100\) is now captured by foreign exporters as quota rents instead of the domestic treasury, widening the domestic nation’s net welfare loss from \(\$50\) to \(B + C + D = \mathbf{\$150}\).

Conclusion: Under the \(\$10\) tariff, domestic consumers lose \(\$275\): \(\$125\) transfers to domestic producers, \(\$100\) goes to government revenue, and \(\$50\) is permanently destroyed as deadweight loss.








NoteOptional Advanced Calculus Extension: Optimal Tariff for a Large Country



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: While a tariff always lowers national welfare for a small price-taking country (\(P_w\) fixed), a large country whose import demand lowers the world price by \(\Delta P_w = P_{w0} - P_{w1} > 0\) gains a terms-of-trade improvement of \(\Delta P_w \times M_t\). Net national welfare changes by \(\Delta W = (\Delta P_w \times M_t) - (B + D)\). Maximizing national welfare by equating domestic marginal benefit \(P(M) = P_w(1 + \tau)\) to the marginal import expenditure \(\frac{d}{dM}[P_w(M)M] = P_w\bigl(1 + \frac{1}{\varepsilon_s^*}\bigr)\) yields the optimal ad valorem tariff rate:
\[
\tau^* = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_s^*}, \qquad \text{where } \varepsilon_s^* = \frac{dM}{dP_w}\frac{P_w}{M} > 0 \text{ is the foreign export supply elasticity.}
\]
For a small open economy, \(\varepsilon_s^* \to \infty\), confirming \(\tau^* = 0\). Even for a large country, this formula assumes foreign trading partners do not retaliate with counter-tariffs—which in practice typically leaves both nations worse off.

section: 2.3 Ricardian Comparative Advantage
text:
2.3 Ricardian Comparative Advantage
Comparative advantage is determined strictly by lower domestic opportunity cost. ::: {.callout-note title=“Terms of Trade Rule”}
Mutually beneficial exchange requires the Terms of Trade (\(TOT\)) to settle strictly between both domestic opportunity cost ratios:
\[
\left|\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}\right|_{\text{Region A}} < TOT < \left|\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}\right|_{\text{Region B}}
\]
Specialization and trade shift the Consumption Possibilities Frontier (\(CPF\)) strictly outside the domestic autarky PPF.
:::

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
text:
The Substitution Effect: As the price of a good rises, it becomes relatively more expensive compared to alternative goods, incentivizing consumers to substitute toward cheaper alternatives.
The Income Effect: A price increase erodes the consumer’s real purchasing power, constraining the total quantity of goods they can afford to purchase.


3.1.1 Direct vs. Inverse Demand
In empirical economics, demand is specified directly as quantity as a function of price:
\[
Q_d = a - bP \quad (a > 0, b > 0)
\]
Because economists traditionally graph price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis (following Alfred Marshall), we invert the equation to obtain the Inverse Demand Function:
\[
P = \frac{a}{b} - \frac{1}{b}Q_d
\]
Here, \(\frac{a}{b}\) represents the choke price—the price at which quantity demanded drops to exactly zero.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
section: 3.2 Shifts in Demand vs. Movements Along the Demand Curve
text:
3.2 Shifts in Demand vs. Movements Along the Demand Curve






NoteCrucial Distinction: Demand vs. Quantity Demanded




Movement Along the Curve (Change in Quantity Demanded): Caused strictly by a change in the good’s own price.
Shift of the Entire Curve (Change in Demand): Caused by changes in non-price determinants, altering quantity demanded at every price level.




3.2.1 Non-Price Determinants of Demand

Consumer Income: For a normal good, demand shifts rightward as income expands (\(\varepsilon_I > 0\)). For an inferior good (such as instant ramen or intercity bus transit), demand shifts leftward as income rises (\(\varepsilon_I < 0\)).
Prices of Related Goods:
Substitutes: An increase in the price of Good \(Y\) shifts demand for Good \(X\) to the right (\(\varepsilon_{xy} > 0\)).
Complements: An increase in the price of Good \(Y\) shifts demand for Good \(X\) to the left (\(\varepsilon_{xy} < 0\)).
Tastes and Preferences: Exogenous shifts in consumer culture, health studies, or advertising.
Buyer Expectations: Anticipated future price increases prompt consumers to accelerate current purchases, shifting current demand rightward.
Market Demographics: An expansion in the population of potential buyers shifts market demand outward.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
section: 3.3 The Nature of Supply and Marginal Opportunity Costs
text:
3.3 The Nature of Supply and Marginal Opportunity Costs
The Law of Supply establishes a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied, ceteris paribus:
\[
P \uparrow \implies Q_s \uparrow, \qquad P \downarrow \implies Q_s \downarrow
\]
Supply slopes upward because production is governed by the Law of Diminishing Marginal Productivity. As firms hire variable factor inputs into fixed plant capacity, the marginal product of labor declines, forcing marginal production costs (\(MC\)) to escalate. To cover higher incremental costs, firms require higher market prices.

3.3.1 Linear Supply Formulations
\[
Q_s = c + dP \iff P = -\frac{c}{d} + \frac{1}{d}Q_s \quad (d > 0)
\]


3.3.2 Non-Price Determinants of Supply
Supply shifts when underlying production parameters change:

Input Prices: Wage increases, raw material inflation, or soaring energy costs increase marginal cost, shifting supply leftward.
Technological Progress: Cost-reducing manufacturing breakthroughs allow firms to produce more output at each price level, shifting supply rightward.
Government Taxes and Subsidies: An excise tax increases per-unit production cost, shifting supply vertically upward by the tax amount \(t\).
Number of Active Producers: Industry entry expands market supply; business closures contract it.

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
section: 3.4 Market Equilibrium and Price Discovery
text:
3.4 Market Equilibrium and Price Discovery
A competitive market attains equilibrium where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied:
\[
Q_d(P^*) = Q_s(P^*) = Q^*
\]






TipStep-by-Step Algebraic Equilibrium Solution



Consider a regional agricultural market for specialty roasted coffee beans: \[Q_d = 500 - 15P, \qquad Q_s = -100 + 15P\] 1. Equate \(Q_d\) and \(Q_s\): \[500 - 15P = -100 + 15P \implies 30P = 600 \implies P^* = \$20\] 2. Substitute \(P^* = \$20\) into either direct schedule: \[Q^* = 500 - 15(20) = 500 - 300 = 200 \text{ bags}\] 3. Verify at disequilibrium prices:

If \(P = \$25\) (Price too high): \(Q_d = 125\), \(Q_s = 275 \implies \text{Surplus} = +150\). Unsold inventory forces price downward.
If \(P = \$15\) (Price too low): \(Q_d = 275\), \(Q_s = 125 \implies \text{Shortage} = -150\). Eager buyers bid price upward.

When demand and supply shift concurrently, exactly one equilibrium variable (\(P^*\) or \(Q^*\)) changes unambiguously, while the other is indeterminate without knowing the exact relative magnitudes of the shifts.

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
text:
Construct and interpret a Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF) to distinguish productively efficient, inefficient, and unattainable output combinations.
Calculate opportunity costs from linear equations and discrete production schedules, and explain why imperfect factor adaptability generates the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost.
Identify the drivers of outward PPF shifts (capital accumulation, labor growth, human capital, and technological progress).
Distinguish absolute advantage from comparative advantage, establish valid Terms of Trade (\(TOT\)) bounds, and prove how trade shifts the Consumption Possibilities Frontier (\(CPF\)) outside the domestic PPF.








TipBring It Home: Why Doesn’t California Grow All Its Own Coffee or Build Every Laptop?



California possesses some of the most productive farmland, engineering talent, and venture capital in the world. Technically, California farms could grow coffee beans in climate-controlled greenhouses, and California factories could assemble every smartphone and laptop sold in the state. Yet California imports virtually all of its coffee from Latin America and consumer electronics from East Asia, while exporting almonds, wine, software, and advanced semiconductor designs. The Production Possibilities Frontier and the principle of comparative advantage explain why doing everything yourself—even when you are good at it—makes everyone poorer.

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: 2.1 Scarcity, Productive Efficiency, and the PPF Model
text:
2.1 Scarcity, Productive Efficiency, and the PPF Model

Conceptual Introduction
In Chapter 1, we saw how an individual student allocates a fixed weekly budget between two goods. Now we zoom out to an entire economy. Every society faces scarcity: its productive inputs—land and natural resources, labor hours, physical capital (machinery, factories, servers), and entrepreneurial ability—are finite at any moment in time. Because resources are limited, producing more of one good requires diverting inputs away from producing something else. Economists capture this fundamental trade-off with the Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF), a curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods or services an economy can produce when all available resources are fully employed using current technology (holding resource supplies and technology fixed, ceteris paribus).
The PPF divides all conceivable production bundles into three distinct zones. Any combination lying on the frontier represents productive efficiency: the economy is squeezing the maximum possible output from its existing inputs, so it is impossible to produce more of one good without giving up some of the other. Any combination lying inside the frontier is attainable but productively inefficient, meaning resources are sitting idle (such as unemployed workers during a recession) or are misallocated across industries. Finally, any combination lying outside the frontier is currently unattainable given existing factor supplies and technology.
Crucially, reaching the frontier is only half of the economic problem. While every point on the PPF is productively efficient, society must still choose which specific point along the curve best satisfies human wants—a criterion known as allocative efficiency. Moving from one efficient point on the PPF to another requires paying an explicit opportunity cost: the quantity of Good \(Y\) that must be forgone to obtain additional units of Good \(X\).






NoteClear It Up: Productive Efficiency vs. Allocative Efficiency




Productive Efficiency means operating on the PPF—producing goods at the lowest possible resource cost without wasting inputs. Every point on the PPF is productively efficient.
Allocative Efficiency means choosing the single point on the PPF that society values most (where marginal benefit equals marginal cost, \(MB = MC\)). An economy producing millions of unwanted cassette tapes at full capacity is productively efficient, yet allocatively inefficient.





Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates a simplified linear Production Possibilities Frontier for an economy allocating fixed resources between Electric Vehicles (\(X\)) and Grid Battery Packs (\(Y\)), under the simplifying assumption that resources are equally adaptable between both industries (generating a constant opportunity cost).



Figure 1. Linear Production Possibilities Frontier. Point \(A\) lies on the frontier and achieves productive efficiency; point \(U\) lies inside the frontier with underutilized capacity; point \(W\) lies outside the frontier and cannot be reached with current resources.








TipReal-World Application: Land and Grid Allocation in California’s Central Valley



California’s Central Valley illustrates a concrete PPF trade-off between utility-scale solar power generation and irrigated specialty agriculture (such as almonds, tomatoes, and pistachios). Both activities compete for flat, sun-drenched acreage, senior water allocations, and high-voltage transmission interconnection capacity. During drought years or transmission bottlenecks, idling farmland without installing solar panels leaves the regional economy at an interior point like \(U\), forfeiting both farm output and clean electricity. Conversely, converting retired agricultural acreage into solar-plus-storage installations moves the region along its frontier toward higher clean-energy output, whereas simultaneously expanding irrigated acreage and solar capacity beyond available water and grid limits (point \(W\)) is physically impossible without new desalination or transmission infrastructure.




Mathematical Foundation
When resources are equally suited to producing both goods, the PPF is a straight line with a constant slope. Suppose an economy’s resource constraint between Electric Vehicles (\(X\), in thousands) and Battery Packs (\(Y\), in thousands) is given by:
\[
2X + Y = 100 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad Y = 100 - 2X
\]
Here, the vertical intercept (\(X = 0 \implies Y = 100\)) shows maximum battery production (\(100\) thousand packs), and the horizontal intercept (\(Y = 0 \implies X = 50\)) shows maximum vehicle production (\(50\) thousand vehicles). The magnitude of the slope measures the constant opportunity cost of producing \(1\) additional unit of \(X\):
\[
\text{Opportunity Cost of } 1X = \left|\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}\right| = 2 \text{ battery packs per electric vehicle}
\]
(Equivalently, \(2\) thousand battery packs per thousand electric vehicles.) Conversely, gaining \(1\) battery pack requires sacrificing \(\frac{1}{2} = 0.5\) electric vehicles.
crumbs: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: 2.2 The Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost and Economic Growth
text:
2.2 The Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost and Economic Growth

Conceptual Introduction
While a straight-line PPF is useful for building intuition, real-world production frontiers bow outward—meaning they are concave to the origin. This curvature reflects the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost: as an economy expands production of one good, the opportunity cost of producing each additional unit rises. Why does this happen? Productive resources are not identical; they exhibit imperfect factor adaptability. Certain parcels of land, specialized machines, and worker skill sets are naturally suited to one industry and poorly suited to another.
When an economy begins shifting resources out of Good \(Y\) (say, agricultural grain) and into Good \(X\) (say, autonomous drones), rational managers first reassign the inputs best adapted to drone manufacturing—such as robotics engineers and precision electronics technicians—while leaving fertile farmland untouched. Initially, drone output rises substantially while grain output barely dips. However, as drone production expands further, the economy must pull in workers and land progressively less suited to aerospace assembly and far more productive in farming, causing the grain sacrificed per additional drone to escalate sharply.
Over longer time horizons, the PPF is not static. Economic growth occurs when an economy expands its productive capacity, shifting the entire PPF outward so previously unattainable bundles become feasible. Four primary forces drive outward PPF shifts: (1) physical capital accumulation (building new factories, power grids, and computing clusters), (2) labor force growth, (3) human capital investment (education, vocational training, and public health), and (4) technological innovation that raises total factor productivity. Notably, an economy that devotes a larger share of current resources to capital goods rather than immediate consumption will experience faster outward PPF expansion in future years.






NoteClear It Up: Economic Recovery vs. Long-Run Economic Growth




Moving from Inside the PPF Toward the Frontier represents short-run recovery—putting unemployed workers and idle factories back to work. The economy’s productive capacity has not expanded; utilization has simply improved.
Shifting the Entire PPF Outward represents long-run economic growth—expanding the economy’s maximum productive potential through new capital, a larger or better-trained workforce, or improved technology.





Visual Representation
Figure 2 shows how equal \(2\)-thousand-unit increases in drone production (\(X\)) require progressively larger sacrifices of grain (\(Y\)) along a bowed-out PPF. Figure 3 contrasts a broad outward expansion from economy-wide capital and technology growth with a sector-biased technological breakthrough in Good \(X\).



Figure 2. Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost. Moving from \(B\) to \(C\) gains \(2\) thousand drones at a cost of \(12\) thousand tons of grain (\(6\) tons per drone), whereas moving from \(D\) to \(E\) gains \(2\) thousand drones at a cost of \(28\) thousand tons of grain (\(14\) tons per drone).





Figure 3. Dynamic Shifts of the Production Possibilities Frontier. Panel (a) shows an economy-wide expansion in resources or general-purpose technology shifting both intercepts outward; Panel (b) shows productivity gains specific to Good \(X\) rotating the horizontal intercept outward.








TipReal-World Application: AI Data Center Buildout vs. Consumer Electronics and Grid Capacity



Rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure illustrates both increasing opportunity cost in the short run and outward frontier shifts in the long run. Semiconductor cleanrooms, high-bandwidth memory fabs, and electrical transformers cannot be built overnight. Reallocating existing wafer capacity and electrical engineers from smartphones and automotive chips into AI server clusters initially taps flexible capacity, but pushing further forces manufacturers to cannibalize specialized industrial lines—sharply driving up the opportunity cost of each additional server rack. Over a multi-year horizon, however, constructing new fabrication plants, training electrical engineers, and deploying next-generation chip lithography expands the economy’s overall capacity, shifting \(\text{PPF}_0\) outward to \(\text{PPF}_1\).




Mathematical Foundation
Table~\(\ref{tab:increasing_oc}\) records the discrete production schedule plotted in Figure 2, generated by the concave frontier \(Y = 100 - X^2\) for \(0 \le X \le 10\) (where \(X\) is measured in thousands of drones and \(Y\) in thousand tons of grain). Over any discrete interval from \((X_1, Y_1)\) to \((X_2, Y_2)\), the per-unit opportunity cost of Good \(X\) is:
\[
\text{Per-Unit Opportunity Cost of } X = \left|\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}\right| = \frac{|Y_2 - Y_1|}{X_2 - X_1}
\]
Because both the numerator (\(\Delta Y\), thousand tons) and denominator (\(\Delta X\), thousand drones) are measured in thousands, the factor of \(1{,}000\) cancels, giving the opportunity cost directly in tons of grain per drone.

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: 2.3 Specialization, Ricardian Comparative Advantage, and Gains from Trade
text:
2.3 Specialization, Ricardian Comparative Advantage, and Gains from Trade

Conceptual Introduction
If every household or region tried to produce everything it consumed in isolation—a state economists call autarky—consumption would be strictly trapped on or inside its own domestic PPF. Yet in reality, individuals, regions, and nations specialize in a narrow range of activities and trade for everything else. Economist David Ricardo proved in 1817 that trade creates mutual gains not because one partner is better at everything, but because trading partners differ in their relative opportunity costs.
To see why, we must separate two concepts that people frequently confuse. A producer has an absolute advantage in a good if it can produce more total output of that good using the same resources (or the same output using fewer inputs). By contrast, a producer has a comparative advantage in a good if it can produce that good at a lower domestic opportunity cost than its trading partner. Because opportunity cost is a ratio (\(\left|\Delta Y / \Delta X\right|\)), it is mathematically impossible for one producer to have a comparative advantage in both goods unless their domestic opportunity costs are identical.
When each region specializes in the good where it holds a comparative advantage and trades at a mutually agreed exchange price—the Terms of Trade (\(TOT\))—both partners can consume combinations of goods that lie strictly outside their domestic PPFs. In graphical terms, specialization and trade pivot a region’s Consumption Possibilities Frontier (\(CPF\)) outward above its autarky PPF, generating net welfare gains for both sides. (The standard Ricardian model makes three simplifying assumptions: constant domestic opportunity costs along linear PPFs, full employment of resources in both regions, and zero transportation or tariff costs.)






NoteClear It Up: Terms of Trade (\(TOT\)) Rule & Absolute Advantage Misconception



Mutually beneficial trade occurs if and only if the Terms of Trade (\(TOT\), expressed as units of Good \(Y\) exchanged per \(1\) unit of Good \(X\)) settle strictly between both regions’ domestic opportunity costs:
\[
\left|\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}\right|_{\text{Exporter of } X} < TOT < \left|\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X}\right|_{\text{Importer of } X}
\]
Even if a high-productivity nation holds an absolute advantage in every single industry (producing more output per worker in both \(X\) and \(Y\)), it still gains from trade by specializing in the sector where its productivity edge is largest—and therefore its domestic opportunity cost is lowest.




Visual Representation
Figure 4 illustrates Ricardian specialization and gains from trade between two regions—NorCal and SoCal—producing Microchips (\(X\)) and Avocados (\(Y\)). By specializing in its comparative-advantage good and trading at \(TOT = 3\) million crates of avocados per million microchips, each region reaches a post-trade consumption bundle (\(T^*\)) strictly beyond its domestic autarky frontier.



Figure 4. Ricardian Specialization and the Consumption Possibilities Frontier (\(CPF\)). Trading at \(TOT = 3Y\text{ per }1X\) pivots both regions’ Consumption Possibilities Frontiers strictly outside their domestic PPFs, allowing both \(T^*_N\) and \(T^*_S\) to exceed autarky consumption in both goods.








TipReal-World Application: Semiconductor Design vs. Advanced Packaging Supply Chains



Modern semiconductor production splits cleanly along comparative advantage lines. Silicon Valley engineering clusters possess deep ecosystems of chip architects and electronic design automation (EDA) software, giving them a low opportunity cost in logic and AI processor design. Meanwhile, East Asian manufacturing hubs possess dense networks of precision cleanrooms, substrate suppliers, and assembly technicians, giving them a much lower opportunity cost in wafer fabrication and advanced chip packaging. Rather than each region attempting to build an isolated end-to-end supply chain in autarky, firms design chips in California, fabricate and package them abroad, and trade completed processors—expanding global computing power far beyond what either region could achieve alone.




Mathematical Foundation
Consider two regions, NorCal and SoCal, each with fixed annual resources capable of producing Microchips (\(X\), in millions) and Avocados (\(Y\), in millions) along linear PPFs:

NorCal PPF: \(Y = 80 - 2X\) (maximum \(40\text{M}\) chips if \(Y = 0\), or \(80\text{M}\) crates of avocados if \(X = 0\)).
SoCal PPF: \(Y = 120 - 4X\) (maximum \(30\text{M}\) chips if \(Y = 0\), or \(120\text{M}\) crates of avocados if \(X = 0\)).







TipBring It Home: Why Specialization Beats Self-Sufficiency



Returning to our opening question: California does not grow its own coffee or assemble every laptop because doing so would force the state to pull scarce land, water, and engineering talent out of sectors where its comparative advantage is highest. By specializing in high-value agriculture, software, and chip design and trading with partners that have lower relative opportunity costs in coffee cultivation and hardware assembly, California pushes its Consumption Possibilities Frontier outward—obtaining more total goods than autarky could ever deliver.

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Production Possibilities Frontier & Gains from Trade
section: Check Your Understanding
text:
Check Your Understanding

Conceptual: Explain why an economy operating inside its PPF does not face an opportunity cost when expanding production of both goods simultaneously, whereas an economy operating on its PPF always faces an opportunity cost.
Linear PPF Analysis: An economy’s PPF between Cloud Servers (\(X\)) and Medical Scanners (\(Y\)) is given by \(Y = 60 - 3X\).
What is the opportunity cost of producing \(1\) Cloud Server? What is the opportunity cost of producing \(1\) Medical Scanner?
Determine whether bundles \((12, 24)\), \((10, 25)\), and \((15, 20)\) are efficient, inefficient, or unattainable.
Comparative Advantage & Trade: Country Alpha can produce either \(50\) tons of Steel (\(X\)) or \(100\) tons of Wheat (\(Y\)) along a linear PPF. Country Beta can produce either \(40\) tons of Steel (\(X\)) or \(40\) tons of Wheat (\(Y\)) along a linear PPF.
Which country has the absolute advantage in Steel? Which has the comparative advantage in Steel?
State the range of mutually beneficial Terms of Trade (\(TOT\)) for \(1\) ton of Steel in terms of Wheat.
If both countries specialize completely and trade \(18\) tons of Steel for \(27\) tons of Wheat (\(TOT = 1.5\)), calculate each country’s post-trade consumption bundle and compare it to autarky bundles \(A_{\text{Alpha}}(15, 70)\) and \(A_{\text{Beta}}(20, 20)\).


Worked Solutions

Inside the PPF, idle or misallocated resources exist; putting unemployed inputs to work increases output of both goods without requiring sacrifices elsewhere. On the PPF, all resources are fully and efficiently employed, so expanding one sector requires withdrawing inputs from the other.
(a) \(\text{OC}_{1X} = 3\) Medical Scanners; \(\text{OC}_{1Y} = \frac{1}{3}\) Cloud Servers. (b) At \(X = 12\), \(Y_{\max} = 60 - 3(12) = 24 \implies (12, 24)\) is efficient; at \(X = 10\), \(Y_{\max} = 30 > 25 \implies (10, 25)\) is inefficient; at \(X = 15\), \(Y_{\max} = 15 < 20 \implies (15, 20)\) is unattainable.
(a) Alpha has absolute advantage in both (\(50 > 40\) Steel; \(100 > 40\) Wheat). Opportunity cost of \(1\) Steel: Alpha \(= \frac{100}{50} = 2\) Wheat; Beta \(= \frac{40}{40} = 1\) Wheat. Beta has comparative advantage in Steel (\(1 < 2\)), and Alpha has comparative advantage in Wheat (\(0.5 < 1\)). (b) \(1\text{ ton Wheat} < TOT_{1\text{ Steel}} < 2\text{ tons Wheat}\). (c) Beta specializes in Steel \((40, 0)\), exports \(18\) Steel for \(27\) Wheat, and consumes \((22, 27)\)—gaining \(+2\) tons of Steel and \(+7\) tons of Wheat over autarky \((20, 20)\), and lying \(9\) tons of Wheat outside Beta’s autarky PPF (\(Y_{\text{PPF}}(22) = 40 - 22 = 18 < 27\)). Alpha specializes in Wheat \((0, 100)\), exports \(27\) Wheat for \(18\) Steel, and consumes \((18, 73)\)—gaining \(+3\) tons of Steel and \(+3\) tons of Wheat over autarky \((15, 70)\), and lying \(9\) tons of Wheat outside Alpha’s autarky PPF (\(Y_{\text{PPF}}(18) = 100 - 2(18) = 64 < 73\)).

title: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism
text:
Conceptual Introduction
In Chapter 2, we used the production possibilities frontier (PPF) to show that when countries specialize according to comparative advantage—producing goods at a lower domestic opportunity cost—and trade, total consumption can expand beyond domestic production limits. Now we bring comparative advantage into a single-market supply-and-demand framework to pinpoint who wins and who loses inside a country when it opens its borders to international trade. Throughout our core graphical and algebraic analysis, we assume a small open economy (the country is a price-taker in the world market and cannot alter the global price), linear domestic supply and demand curves, competitive markets, and zero transportation costs (ceteris paribus).
To determine whether a small open economy becomes an importer or an exporter of a specific good, compare its autarky (no-trade) domestic equilibrium price (\(P_A\)) against the prevailing world price (\(P_w\)):

Importing Country (\(P_w < P_A\)): Foreign producers have a comparative advantage and can supply the good at a lower opportunity cost than domestic firms. Under free trade, the domestic price drops from \(P_A\) to \(P_w\). Domestic consumers benefit—buying more at a lower price and capturing a large expansion in Consumer Surplus (\(CS\)). Domestic producers are harmed—cutting production and losing Producer Surplus (\(PS\)). Crucially, the gain to consumers strictly exceeds the loss to domestic producers, creating a net gain in Total Social Surplus (\(TS = CS + PS\)).
Exporting Country (\(P_w > P_A\)): Domestic producers have a comparative advantage and can sell abroad at a higher world price. Under free trade, the domestic price rises from \(P_A\) to \(P_w\). Domestic producers expand output and capture a gain in Producer Surplus that strictly exceeds the loss in Consumer Surplus suffered by domestic buyers—once again generating a positive net gain in Total Social Surplus.

This sharp distributional split explains why trade policy is perpetually contentious in real-world markets such as global apparel, consumer electronics, and agricultural exports. When households buy smartphones, laptops, and clothing sourced from specialized global supply chains at lower world prices, the gains from free trade are spread thinly across millions of consumers (for example, saving \(\$30\) on a pair of shoes). By contrast, the losses from import competition are concentrated among specific domestic factories and workers, giving import-competing industries a strong incentive to lobby for trade barriers even when free trade expands total national surplus.






NoteClear It Up: Do Imports Subtract from National Welfare Because Domestic Producers Lose?



A common misconception is that exports are always good'' for an economy while imports arebad’’ because imports reduce domestic producer surplus in the competing industry. In welfare economics, both exporting and importing raise Total Social Surplus. When a country imports at \(P_w < P_A\), domestic consumers gain more surplus than domestic producers lose (\(\Delta CS + \Delta PS = \Delta TS > 0\)), and domestic labor and capital are freed to move toward sectors where the country holds a comparative advantage.




Visual Representation
Figure 1 illustrates an importing market where the world price \(P_w = \$40\) lies below the autarky price \(P_A = \$60\), expanding Total Social Surplus by the shaded teal triangle. Table~\(\ref{tab:free_trade_summary}\) summarizes how both importing and exporting reshape domestic prices and surplus.



Figure 1. Welfare Gains from Free Trade (Importing Case). When \(P_w = \$40 < P_A = \$60\), domestic production falls from \(20\) to \(10\) tons and domestic consumption rises from \(20\) to \(30\) tons, generating \(20\) tons of imports and a net gain in Total Social Surplus (shaded teal triangle).




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra-First)
Assuming linear domestic demand and supply in a small open economy, trade volumes and net social surplus gains are computed directly using triangle areas:
\[
\text{Importing } (P_w < P_A): \quad \text{Imports} = Q_d(P_w) - Q_s(P_w), \qquad \Delta TS_{\text{import}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Imports} \times (P_A - P_w)
\]
\[
\text{Exporting } (P_w > P_A): \quad \text{Exports} = Q_s(P_w) - Q_d(P_w), \qquad \Delta TS_{\text{export}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Exports} \times (P_w - P_A)
\]






NoteWork It Out 14.1: Free Trade Surplus in a Small Steel Market



In a small open economy’s market for steel, domestic inverse demand is \(P = 100 - 2Q_d\) and domestic inverse supply is \(P = 20 + 2Q_s\), where \(P\) is measured in dollars per ton and \(Q\) in tons.

Find the autarky equilibrium price \(P_A\), quantity \(Q_A\), and autarky surplus (\(CS_A\), \(PS_A\), \(TS_A\)).
Suppose the country opens to free trade at a world price of \(P_w = \$40\) per ton. Calculate domestic quantity supplied, domestic quantity demanded, import volume, \(\Delta CS\), \(\Delta PS\), and the net gain in Total Social Surplus (\(\Delta TS\)).
Exporting Check: What would happen to trade volume and \(\Delta TS\) if the world price were instead \(P_w = \$80\) per ton?

Step-by-Step Solution:

Autarky Equilibrium (\(P_A, Q_A\)) and Autarky Surplus: Set inverse demand equal to inverse supply (\(Q_d = Q_s = Q_A\)):

\[
100 - 2Q_A = 20 + 2Q_A \implies 80 = 4Q_A \implies Q_A = \mathbf{20\text{ tons}}, \qquad P_A = 100 - 2(20) = \mathbf{\$60}
\]
Using the vertical intercepts (\(\$100\) for demand and \(\$20\) for supply):
\[
CS_A = \frac{1}{2}(20)(\$100 - \$60) = \$400, \qquad PS_A = \frac{1}{2}(20)(\$60 - \$20) = \$400, \qquad TS_A = \mathbf{\$800}
\]

Importing Equilibrium at \(P_w = \$40\):

\[
40 = 20 + 2Q_s \implies 2Q_s = 20 \implies Q_s = \mathbf{10\text{ tons produced domestically}}
\]
\[
40 = 100 - 2Q_d \implies 2Q_d = 60 \implies Q_d = \mathbf{30\text{ tons consumed domestically}}
\]
\[
\text{Imports} = Q_d - Q_s = 30 - 10 = \mathbf{20\text{ tons}}
\]
Compute free-trade Consumer and Producer Surplus:
\[
CS_{\text{trade}} = \frac{1}{2}(30)(\$100 - \$40) = \$900 \implies \Delta CS = \$900 - \$400 = \mathbf{+\$500}
\]
\[
PS_{\text{trade}} = \frac{1}{2}(10)(\$40 - \$20) = \$100 \implies \Delta PS = \$100 - \$400 = \mathbf{-\$300}
\]
Verify Net Social Surplus Gain two ways:
\[
\Delta TS = \Delta CS + \Delta PS = +\$500 - \$300 = \mathbf{+\$200}
\]
\[
\Delta TS = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Imports} \times (P_A - P_w) = \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times (\$60 - \$40) = 10 \times \$20 = \mathbf{+\$200}
\]

Exporting Check at \(P_w = \$80\): Since \(P_w = \$80 > P_A = \$60\), the country becomes an exporter:

\[
80 = 20 + 2Q_s \implies Q_s = 30\text{ tons}, \qquad 80 = 100 - 2Q_d \implies Q_d = 10\text{ tons}
\]
\[
\text{Exports} = Q_s - Q_d = 30 - 10 = \mathbf{20\text{ tons}}
\]
Here \(CS_{\text{exp}} = \frac{1}{2}(10)(100 - 80) = \$100\) (\(\Delta CS = -\$300\)) and \(PS_{\text{exp}} = \frac{1}{2}(30)(80 - 20) = \$900\) (\(\Delta PS = +\$500\)), yielding the exact same net gain \(\Delta TS = \frac{1}{2}(20)(\$80 - \$60) = \mathbf{+\$200}\).
Conclusion: Opening to free trade raises national social welfare by \(+\$200\) whether the country imports at \(\$40\) or exports at \(\$80\), though the domestic winners and losers flip between the two cases.








NoteOptional Advanced Calculus Extension: Integral Form of Gains from Trade



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: For general (possibly nonlinear) domestic demand \(Q_d(P)\) and supply \(Q_s(P)\), welfare changes under importing (\(P_w < P_A\)) are exact definite integrals with respect to price:
\[
\Delta CS = \int_{P_w}^{P_A} Q_d(P)\,dP, \qquad \Delta PS = -\int_{P_w}^{P_A} Q_s(P)\,dP, \qquad \Delta TS = \int_{P_w}^{P_A} \bigl[Q_d(P) - Q_s(P)\bigr]\,dP.
\]
In our steel market, inverting the linear curves gives \(Q_d(P) = 50 - 0.5P\) and \(Q_s(P) = 0.5P - 10\), so import demand is \(M(P) = Q_d(P) - Q_s(P) = 60 - P\). Integrating from \(P_w = 40\) to \(P_A = 60\) confirms our geometric triangle:
\[
\Delta TS = \int_{40}^{60} (60 - P)\,dP = \left[60P - \frac{1}{2}P^2\right]_{40}^{60} = (3{,}600 - 1{,}800) - (2{,}400 - 800) = 1{,}800 - 1{,}600 = +\$200.
\]

title: 14  Chapter 14: International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism
section: 14.3 Arguments for Protectionism and Trade Policy Evaluation
text:
14.3 Arguments for Protectionism and Trade Policy Evaluation

Conceptual Introduction
If tariffs and import quotas strictly reduce Total Social Surplus in a small open economy, why do governments routinely enact them? Beyond lobbying by concentrated producer groups, policymakers cite four primary arguments for trade protection, each carrying important economic trade-offs:

National Security: Preserving domestic production capacity in defense-critical sectors (such as specialty steel, semiconductors, or aerospace) reduces vulnerability during geopolitical disruptions. Economists caution, however, that industries routinely stretch the ``national security’’ label to secure protection even when stockpiling or allied sourcing is far cheaper.
Infant Industry: Temporarily shielding a young domestic industry may help firms achieve economies of scale and learning-by-doing until they can compete globally. In practice, governments struggle to pick future winners, and ``temporary’’ tariffs often become politically entrenched long after the industry matures.
Anti-Dumping (Unfair Competition): Dumping occurs when a foreign firm exports a product below its cost of production or below its home-market price. While tariffs can deter predatory pricing designed to drive domestic rivals out of business, anti-dumping complaints are frequently filed against foreign competitors that are simply more efficient.
Protecting Domestic Jobs and Wages: Import barriers can save visible jobs inside a protected factory, but they do not increase net economy-wide employment. Higher prices for protected inputs reduce demand and employment in downstream and export-oriented industries, often resulting in a very high consumer cost per job saved.

To avoid destructive tit-for-tat tariff wars—a classic Prisoner’s Dilemma where unilateral protection leaves every trading partner worse off—nations participate in multilateral institutions such as the World Trade Organization (WTO) and regional free trade agreements (such as the USMCA). Economists also distinguish between whether to help displaced workers and how to help them: targeted domestic policies (such as worker retraining, relocation assistance, or direct production subsidies for genuinely strategic goods) avoid distorting consumer prices and impose far lower deadweight loss than broad border tariffs.


Visual Representation
Figure 3 decomposes the \(\$275\) Consumer Surplus loss from our \(\$10\) steel tariff and contrasts its \(\$50\) deadweight loss against a \(\$10\) per-ton domestic production subsidy that achieves the exact same \(+5\)-ton increase in domestic steel output while cutting deadweight loss in half.



Figure 3. Policy Evaluation of the \(\$10\) Steel Tariff. Panel A decomposes the \(\$275\) consumer loss into producer transfers (\(\$125\)), tariff revenue or quota rents (\(\$100\)), and deadweight loss (\(\$50\)). Panel B shows that a \(\$10\) domestic production subsidy achieves the exact same \(+5\)-ton domestic output increase while eliminating consumption deadweight loss (Triangle \(D\)), halving total deadweight loss to \(\$25\).




Mathematical Foundation (Algebra-First)
To evaluate the economic efficiency of job-protection arguments, economists divide the consumer burden and deadweight loss of a trade barrier by the number of domestic jobs protected (\(\Delta L_{\text{protected}}\)):
\[
\text{Consumer Cost per Job Protected} = \frac{|\Delta CS|}{\Delta L_{\text{protected}}}, \qquad \text{Deadweight Loss per Job Protected} = \frac{B + D}{\Delta L_{\text{protected}}}
\]






NoteWork It Out 14.3: Calculating Consumer Cost per Job Protected



Suppose our steel market in Work It Out 14.2 is scaled to thousands of tons (\(P\) remains in dollars per ton), so the \(\$10\) per-unit tariff expands domestic production by \(\Delta Q_s = 5{,}000\) tons, reduces Consumer Surplus by \(|\Delta CS| = \$275{,}000\), raises Producer Surplus by \(\$125{,}000\), generates \(\$100{,}000\) in tariff revenue, and creates \(\$50{,}000\) in deadweight loss. Assume, as a hypothetical illustration, that producing those extra \(5{,}000\) tons preserves \(\Delta L_{\text{protected}} = 5\) domestic steelworker jobs.

Calculate the consumer cost per job protected.
Calculate the producer surplus gain per job protected and the pure deadweight loss per job protected.
Interpret why consumers pay substantially more per job than domestic steel producers receive.

Step-by-Step Solution:

Consumer Cost per Job Protected:

\[
\frac{|\Delta CS|}{\Delta L_{\text{protected}}} = \frac{\$275{,}000}{5\text{ jobs}} = \mathbf{\$55{,}000\text{ per job}}
\]

Producer Surplus Gain and Deadweight Loss per Job Protected:

\[
\text{Producer Surplus Gain per Job} = \frac{\$125{,}000}{5} = \mathbf{\$25{,}000\text{ per job}}
\]
\[
\text{Deadweight Loss per Job} = \frac{\$50{,}000}{5} = \mathbf{\$10{,}000\text{ per job}}
\]

Economic Interpretation: Consumers bear \(\$55{,}000\) in higher steel costs for every protected job, yet only \(\$25{,}000\) reaches domestic steel producers as surplus (while \(\$20{,}000\) goes to tariff revenue and \(\$10{,}000\) vanishes into deadweight loss). Moreover, if higher steel prices eliminate jobs in downstream industries such as auto manufacturing, the net domestic employment gain is even smaller.









NoteOptional Advanced Calculus Extension: The Targeting Principle (Subsidy vs. Tariff)



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Suppose policymakers seek to raise domestic steel production from \(Q_{s1} = 10\) to \(Q_{s2} = 15\) tons for national security. Instead of a \(\$10\) tariff, consider a direct domestic production subsidy of \(s = \$10\) per ton. Domestic firms receive \(P_w + s = \$50\) and produce \(15\) tons (\(\Delta PS = +\$125\)), while domestic consumers still pay \(P_w = \$40\) and buy \(30\) tons (\(\Delta CS = \$0\)). Government subsidy expenditure is \(s \times Q_{s2} = \$10 \times 15 = \$150\), so net social surplus changes by:
\[
\Delta TS_{\text{subsidy}} = \Delta CS + \Delta PS - s Q_{s2} = 0 + \$125 - \$150 = -\$25 = -\text{Area } B.
\]
More generally, differentiating total surplus with respect to a tariff \(t\) versus a production subsidy \(s\) shows that marginal deadweight loss satisfies:
\[
\frac{d(DWL_{\text{tariff}})}{dt} = t\bigl[Q_s'(P_w + t) - Q_d'(P_w + t)\bigr] \;>\; s\,Q_s'(P_w + s) = \frac{d(DWL_{\text{subsidy}})}{ds} \quad (\text{at } t = s > 0, \text{ since } Q_d' < 0).
\]
Because the subsidy directly targets the production goal without raising the consumer price, it eliminates consumption distortion Triangle \(D\) and strictly dominates the tariff in welfare terms.








TipBring It Home: Weighing Concentrated Producer Gains Against Dispersed Consumer Costs



Returning to the debate between domestic steelworkers and automakers, our surplus framework reveals why trade disputes are so hard to resolve politically. A steel tariff delivers immediate, visible producer gains (Area \(A\)) to domestic mills and their workforce, while spreading a larger consumer loss (\(A + B + C + D\)) across millions of households and downstream manufacturers. Because society as a whole loses deadweight loss (\(B + D\))—and loses even more (\(B + C + D\)) if an import quota hands quota rents to foreign exporters—economists generally recommend keeping trade open while supporting displaced workers directly through retraining and adjustment policies rather than restricting imports.
